              PART A

              Comprehensive review of the course content (Classes 1 to 7)

              A1. Class 1

              Introduction to Preventative Monitoring (Monday, September 14, 2026)

              A1.1 Lesson 1.1

              The course outline and the competency it is built on

              The course outline is a formal document issued under the College's ISEP (Institutional Student Evaluation Policy). Once issued, it binds the instructor as much as the student: no evaluation can be added and no weighting changed without the procedure the policy sets out. Read it as an engineer reads a specification. The full policy is on the Dawson College website.

              Ponderation 2-3-1. The three numbers describe how a Québec college course spends its hours each week: 2 hours of theory, 3 hours of laboratory or practical work, 1 hour of personal study. Together they produce the 75 course hours and the 2 2/3 credits. The ratio says this is a practical course.

              Competency EZ01 — "Monitor a computer network from a cybersecurity perspective." A Québec AEC (Attestation of College Studies) program is built from competencies published by the Ministère de l'Enseignement supérieur and reproduced without alteration in every outline. This course addresses EZ01 in its entirety. Three structural parts sit under the statement:

              • Elements of the competency — the five sub-abilities: (1) distinguish between the concepts linked to cybersecurity; (2) analyze the topology of the network; (3) install and configure surveillance tools; (4) detect and diagnose anomalies; (5) optimize surveillance tools.
              • Performance criteria — the observable standards used for grading; "accurate interpretation of available data" is a criterion, "you did a good job" is not. For the competency as a whole: respect for professional ethics; effective priority management; effective communication with stakeholders; considering various sources of information; accurate interpretation of available data; respect for the confidentiality of the monitoring data collected.
              • Achievement context — the conditions of demonstration: an entire documented network of various platforms; ongoing monitoring; under supervision; in collaboration with other technicians and network users; based on policies, norms and standards and on descriptive infrastructure documents; with the help of technical manuals, equipment, tools and software, script language and network protocols.

              The two constraints written into the context shape the whole course: the network is documented, and the work is collaborative. That is why Lab 1 asks for documentation before anything is installed, and why reporting to stakeholders is graded.

              The six topics, in dependency order. Each topic produces an input the next one consumes:

              # Topic What it produces EZ01 element
              1 Foundations of cybersecurity A shared vocabulary; the ability to tell a security problem from a performance problem 1
              2 Understanding the network to be monitored An inventory, a topology diagram, a prioritized list of monitoring needs 2
              3 Monitoring tools A selected, installed, configured tool with a baseline and alert rules 3
              4 Collecting and analyzing monitoring data Filtered, searchable event and traffic data 4
              5 Detecting and diagnosing anomalies A triaged alert, an analysis, a diagnosis, a written report 4
              6 Optimizing the monitoring setup An updated baseline, fewer false alarms, written recommendations 5

              You cannot prioritize what you have not inventoried; you cannot configure an alert without a baseline; you cannot diagnose an anomaly without data.

              Where the course sits. 420-1C1-DW is a prerequisite for Cyber Defense (420-2C1-DW) and Compliance Assessments (420-2C2-DW) in Term 2, Intrusion Test (420-3C2-DW) in Term 3, and Implementation and Management of Corporate Cybersecurity Measures (420-4C2-DW) in Term 4. Section 7.1 of the Cyber.SoHo Acceptable Use Policy calls the program an escalation: here you observe a network; later you scan it, test it and handle live malicious code. The rule: finishing a course extends your responsibility, never your permissions.

              The job behind the competency. EZ01 describes the entry-level work of a SOC (Security Operations Centre) analyst, also called monitoring technician or Tier 1 analyst: watch a queue of alerts, decide which are real, gather evidence, close or escalate with a written justification. The dominant tool is the SIEM (Security Information and Event Management) platform, which collects log records from many systems into one searchable store and raises alerts from rules.

              Applied example 1.1 — the monitoring scope register of Atelier Nord-Ouest (fictional fourteen-person architectural drafting and printing studio in Verdun, Montréal). A scope register lists every asset to be monitored, why it is monitored, which EZ01 element the work demonstrates, and the evidence handed in. It prevents the two classic engagement failures: an important asset nobody watched, and an asset the client wrongly believed was watched. The program ez01_scope_register.py checks that all five elements are covered and writes the register as a CSV (Comma-Separated Values) file. Section 6.4 of the Acceptable Use Policy requires fictional organizations; section 7.9 requires written authorization (Annex D template) before any real network is touched.

              A1.2 Lesson 1.2

              The schedule and the evaluation plan

              • Dates: Monday, September 14 to Monday, October 19, 2026 — 19 classes in six weeks (an intensive format: the 75 hours of a fifteen-week course delivered in six). Classes meet Monday, Thursday and Friday 18:00–22:00 and Saturday 14:00–18:00. Two statutory closures: Monday, October 5 (Québec provincial election) and Monday, October 12 (Thanksgiving).
              • On campus: only the mid-term (Thursday, October 1) and the final (Monday, October 19). Everything else is online, including all quizzes, all laboratories and the two review sessions (September 28 and October 17).
              Component Dates Each Total
              Four quizzes, online, cumulative Sept 19 · Sept 26 · Oct 10 · Oct 15 5 % 20 %
              Three laboratories, online, one Integrative Project in three parts Sept 25 · Oct 3 · Oct 16 5 % 15 %
              Mid-term examination, in class October 1 — 25 %
              Final examination, in class, summative October 19 — 40 %
              Total 100 %
              • Cumulative quizzes. Each quiz covers all material up to its date. The design relies on retrieval practice (the testing effect) and spaced repetition.
              • Formative versus summative. Formative assessment produces feedback and does not determine the grade; summative assessment measures achievement at the end and does. The final examination is the summative element.
              • The two pass rules. Rule 1: at least 60 % on the final examination; below 60 %, the course is failed and the grade recorded for the whole course becomes that examination grade (88 % accumulated and 52 % on the final gives 52 %, not 73 %). Rule 2: at least 60 % overall. Both rules must hold.
              • The three laboratories are one Integrative Project: Lab 1 maps a network and writes its monitoring plan; Lab 2 installs and configures a tool on that network, builds the baseline and sets the alerts; Lab 3 detects, diagnoses and reports an anomaly and proposes optimizations. Each part is graded at 5 %; assembling the three into one document is optional and formative.
              • Administrative rules: late submissions lose 10 % per day, nothing accepted after seven days; missed tests need a valid reason, no medical certificate for an absence of five days or less, a certificate above five days; literacy: up to 10 % may be deducted for grammar, spelling, punctuation or syntax, and work may be sent back; cheating and plagiarism result in failure of the assignment, the component or the course and are reported in writing to the Dean; quizzes, examinations, sample solutions, rubrics, laboratory virtual machines and credentials are confidential under section 17.2 of the Legal Notice.
              • Required reading account: a free account with the BAnQ (Bibliothèque et Archives nationales du Québec) gives free access to the O'Reilly technical library and LinkedIn Learning.

              Applied example 1.2 — the delivery plan. A course schedule and a project schedule are the same kind of object: dated commitments with dependencies and consequences for slipping. Nothing can be installed until the network is documented; no alert can be tuned until a baseline has been collected, and a baseline needs calendar time (seven days of observation takes seven days); no report can be written until an anomaly has been analyzed. The program term_planner.py verifies that the weights sum to 100 %, computes the running weighted total and the mark still needed on the final, and applies the two pass rules.

              A1.3 Lesson 1.3

              What preventative monitoring actually is

              Definition (learn it word for word): Preventative monitoring is the continuous and systematic observation of a computer network and its systems, carried out in order to detect and report deviations from a known normal state early enough for action to be taken before damage occurs.

              • Continuous: observation runs at all times, not at intervals a technician chooses.
              • Systematic: what is observed, how often and what counts as notable are decided in advance and written down.
              • A known normal state: the baseline, also called the reference database. Without it no observation can be classified: "unusual" has no meaning until "usual" has been measured.
              • Detect and report: detection without reporting changes nothing.
              • Before damage occurs: the observation prevents nothing by itself; it buys the time in which someone else can act.

              A distinction students are marked down for confusing. Controls are classified by when they act: a preventive control stops an event (firewall rule, account lockout, door lock); a detective control records that an event happened (log, alert, camera); a corrective control restores the state afterwards (restore from backup, patch). Monitoring is a detective control. It is called preventative monitoring because it aims at an early stage of an attack, where detection still leaves time to prevent the damage. Write it that way in reports.

              The CIA (Confidentiality, Integrity, Availability) triad — what is protected, how each property fails, and what evidence reveals it:

              Property Definition Typical failure at Atelier Nord-Ouest Evidence that reveals it
              Confidentiality Information is disclosed only to those authorized to receive it A drawing folder copied to an unknown external address Outbound traffic volume and destination in flow records
              Integrity Information is modified only in authorized, recorded ways Drawing files silently altered or encrypted File integrity checks, sudden mass file-write events
              Availability Information and services are accessible when needed The backup service stops and no one is told Service status checks, absence of expected log entries

              The absence of an expected event is itself evidence: a backup server that stopped writing its nightly success message is failing, and a configuration that only alerts on events never sees it.

              Security issue or performance issue? The same symptom can come from either (a saturated link: a large legitimate transfer, or a workstation exfiltrating data). The distinguishing question is not what changed but whether the change is explained. A performance issue has an owner, a cause and usually a change record; a security issue does not.

              The seven-stage monitoring pipeline (the remaining topics are its stages): collect → normalize → baseline → detect → triage → diagnose → report and optimize. Normalizing puts records of different formats into one structure and on one clock: NTP (Network Time Protocol) synchronization is a prerequisite, because systems whose clocks disagree produce evidence that cannot be correlated. Stage 7 feeds back into stage 3, which makes it a cycle.

              Where observations come from:

              Source What it records Format
              Operating system event logs Logons, privilege use, service starts and stops, policy changes Windows Event Log (.evtx); Linux syslog and journald
              Full packet capture Every byte of observed traffic, headers and payload PCAP (Packet Capture) files, read with tools such as Wireshark
              Flow records Who spoke to whom, on which port, for how long, how many bytes — no payload NetFlow and IPFIX (Internet Protocol Flow Information Export)
              Device metrics Processor, memory, disk, interface counters, temperatures SNMP (Simple Network Management Protocol) polling, or agent metrics
              Application and service logs Web requests, database errors, backup job results Plain text, JSON (JavaScript Object Notation), vendor formats
              File integrity records Cryptographic hashes of files, compared over time SHA-256 (Secure Hash Algorithm, 256-bit) digests

              Flow records contain no payload, so they are far smaller and far less privacy-invasive than full capture while still answering most investigative questions: in a small network, flow records plus event logs answer perhaps nine questions in ten.

              The statistics of a baseline. A baseline is a statistical description, not a screenshot of a normal day. For a numeric measurement (failed logons per hour) you record many observations over a representative period and compute the arithmetic mean μ (centre of normal behaviour) and the standard deviation σ (how much normal behaviour varies). A common threshold is μ + 3σ: for an approximately normal distribution about 99.7 % of normal observations fall within three standard deviations of the mean, so a higher value is rare enough to deserve attention. Three is a working convention: raise it and you miss real events (false negatives); lower it and you drown in false alarms (false positives). Two qualifications: the baseline must cover a representative period (daily and weekly cycles — a Tuesday-afternoon baseline alarms every Monday morning), and it must be rebuilt when the network legitimately changes (criterion 5.1, "comprehensive update of reference databases": a stale baseline gives confident, wrong answers).

              How detection quality is measured:

              Term Meaning Cost when high
              TP (true positive) An alert that corresponds to a real event None; this is the goal
              FP (false positive) An alert with no real event behind it Analyst time, then alert fatigue (genuine alerts dismissed by habit)
              FN (false negative) A real event that produced no alert The incident proceeds undetected
              MTTD (mean time to detect) Average interval between an event starting and its detection Proportional to the damage an intruder can do
              MTTR (mean time to respond) Average interval between detection and containment Extends the same window

              The published frameworks this course follows: NIST SP 800-137, Information Security Continuous Monitoring (the foundational specification of ISCM (Information Security Continuous Monitoring), published by the United States National Institute of Standards and Technology); the NIST Cybersecurity Framework (its Detect function is this course); the CIS (Center for Internet Security) Critical Security Controls (Control 8 audit log management, Control 13 network monitoring and defence); MITRE ATT&CK (a public catalogue of adversary techniques with the data sources that detect each one); and, for Canada, the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security (baseline controls and advisories for small and medium organizations).

              Monitoring data is personal information. A record that a user authenticated from a given address at 03:12 is information about a person. In Québec this brings monitoring within the Act respecting the protection of personal information in the private sector as amended by Law 25, supervised by the Commission d'accès à l'information du Québec (CAI), and within articles 35 to 41 of the Civil Code of Québec on respect for private life. Capturing traffic on a network you share with other people can be interception of a private communication under section 184 of the Criminal Code. Operational consequences (sections 6.7 and 7.2 of the Acceptable Use Policy): collect the minimum, keep it in the laboratory, never enable promiscuous or monitor mode on a shared network, delete captured data once the exercise is marked.

              Applied example 1.3 — baselining failed logons on the Atelier Nord-Ouest file server: 168 hourly counts (one week), μ and σ, threshold μ + 3σ, then a day of live observation walked hour by hour; flagged hours are triaged by checking whether they share a source address or account. Failed authentications are a good first measurement because they are noisy in a harmless way (mistyped passwords, a phone holding an old credential), which is why the fixed rule "alert on any failed logon" is useless and the count per hour compared with its own history is informative.

              A1.4 Lesson 1.4

              Building the laboratory environment

              Authorized Lab Environment (Acceptable Use Policy definition; all three conditions must hold at once): (1) you own the environment or are expressly permitted to use it for the exercise; (2) it is disconnected from, or securely segregated from, any production, institutional, corporate, public or third-party network; (3) it contains no real personal data and no system belonging to anyone who has not consented in writing. Condition 2 is the one students break by accident, by leaving a virtual network adapter in bridged mode: the virtual machine is then on your home or campus network like another physical computer, and a capture inside your "laboratory" becomes a capture of other people's traffic — a potential offence under section 184. Nothing on the screen tells you this happened; that is why the pre-flight check exists.

              Vocabulary of virtualization: host (the physical computer and its operating system), guest (an operating system running inside a virtual machine), hypervisor (creates and runs virtual machines; type 1 runs directly on the hardware, type 2 runs as an application — VirtualBox and VMware Workstation are type 2), VM (Virtual Machine) (a complete simulated computer stored on the host as a set of files), ISO image (byte-for-byte contents of an installation disc), snapshot (a saved copy of a machine's complete state at one moment; restoring it discards everything since), virtual network adapter (a simulated NIC (Network Interface Card); its mode is the single most important security setting of the laboratory).

              The five network modes:

              Mode VM reaches the Internet VM reaches other lab VMs VM exposed to your real network Use in this course
              NAT (Network Address Translation) Yes No No inbound Only to download updates, then switch off
              NAT Network Yes Yes No inbound Only when an exercise says so
              Bridged adapter Yes Yes Yes, fully Prohibited
              Host-only adapter No Yes No Permitted (Class 2 calls it the standard mode for lab traffic)
              Internal network No Yes No Preferred for the strictest isolation

              An internal network is a virtual switch that exists only between virtual machines; even the host cannot see its traffic unless it joins deliberately. A host-only adapter adds a link between the host and the virtual machines (convenient to reach a monitoring console from your browser) and still cannot reach the outside world.

              Requirements before Thursday, September 17: RAM (Random Access Memory) 8 GB minimum, 16 GB recommended (three small virtual machines need roughly 6 GB); free disk 80 GB minimum, 120 GB recommended (snapshots consume space); processor virtualization Intel VT-x or AMD-V enabled in the UEFI (Unified Extensible Firmware Interface) or BIOS (Basic Input/Output System) setup screen, not in the operating system; hypervisor Oracle VirtualBox 7.x (the matching Extension Pack only if an exercise requires it); Linux guest Ubuntu Server LTS (Long Term Support); Windows guest: a Microsoft evaluation image provided through the course.

              Verify every download. Publishers publish a SHA-256 checksum next to the download; compute it locally (Get-FileHash .\ubuntu-server.iso -Algorithm SHA256 in PowerShell; sha256sum ubuntu-server.iso or shasum -a 256 on Linux or macOS) and compare before installing. Annex C also asks you to submit unfamiliar links and files to VirusTotal and to check domains with Google Safe Browsing. A clean result is not a guarantee; an unexplained detection is a reason to stop.

              The three machines of the Class 1 plan: AN-FS01 (file server, Windows Server evaluation, 2048 MB, internal network atelier-lan); AN-BK01 (backup server, Ubuntu Server LTS, 1024 MB, internal atelier-lan); AN-MON01 (monitoring station, Ubuntu Server LTS, 2048 MB, internal atelier-lan plus host-only for the console). Take a snapshot as soon as installation finishes and before any exercise, named with the date and what it represents (2026-09-17_clean-install); section 6.4 requires it, and a snapshot turns a lost evening into a thirty-second restore.

              Your equipment, your risk (section 10.3): you accept the risks of running this software — data loss, file-system corruption, crashes, loss of connectivity, unexpected charges from cloud providers. Back up your personal data first; do not run laboratory work on a computer you cannot afford to reinstall.

              Applied example 1.4 — the pre-flight conformity check (deliverable D4, attached to every lab). The script lab_preflight.sh (PowerShell version for Windows hosts) asks the hypervisor for each machine's adapter modes and snapshot list, checks free disk space and prints a conformity verdict; any adapter in bridged mode fails the whole report. The five checks: adapter modes on every lab machine (segregation, condition 2); a snapshot for every machine (recoverability, section 6.4); free disk space above the threshold (stability: a full disk corrupts snapshots); no real personal data on the lab volume (condition 3, sections 6.7 and 18.2); a signed Annex A on file (section 2.2: one signed copy per course before laboratory access). The exercise deliberately finds a fault, because a check that always passes teaches nothing.

              A2. Class 2

              Foundations of Cybersecurity, part 1 (Thursday, September 17, 2026)

              Fictional organization of this class: Grey Pine Bookkeeping, nine people in Montréal, about two hundred clients. Three deliverables: D1 the asset register (Lesson 1), D2 the rating worksheet and file baseline (Lesson 2), D3 the lab readiness report (Lesson 3).

              A2.1 Lesson 1.1

              What cybersecurity is and why organizations need it

              Definition: cybersecurity is the protection of computers, networks, programs and digital information against six unwanted actions — unauthorized access, use, disclosure, disruption, modification and destruction — obtained by combining technologies, written procedures and the daily practices of people. The wording follows the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security and the NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology) glossary. Three neighbouring expressions: information security (every form, paper and speech included), IT (information technology) security (equipment and software), cybersecurity (what is digital and connected to a network — the scope of this course). The centre of the definition is the word unauthorized: the same action is normal when the right person does it and harmful when another person does it. Security work begins with one question: who is allowed to do what, on which system?

              The vocabulary of risk — five words in order: an asset (anything of value that needs protection: information, equipment, a service, an account); a threat (a possible cause of an unwanted event; intentional, accidental or natural/technical; the person or group behind an intentional threat is a threat actor); a vulnerability (a weakness a threat can use: unsupported software, a shared password, an untested backup, an untrained employee); a risk (the combination of the likelihood that a threat uses a vulnerability and the impact if it happens; in a simple qualitative method, risk = likelihood × impact, each rated from 1 to 5); a control (a measure that reduces a risk: technical, administrative or physical). No organization brings every risk to zero; the highest risks are treated first.

              Event, alert, incident. An event is any observable occurrence (a sign-in, a file opened, a refused connection, a disk at 80 %); an alert is a message produced by a tool when events match a configured rule; an incident is an event or group of events that harms or threatens information or systems, or breaks a security rule. An alert is a question; after analysis, the technician decides whether it describes an incident. Security activities fall into prevention, detection and response; preventative monitoring is a detection activity carried out early enough to have a preventive effect.

              Five reasons every organization needs cybersecurity, with Canadian figures from Statistics Canada: (1) the work depends on digital systems — in 2021, about four impacted businesses in ten lost working time, 36 hours on average; (2) incidents are frequent and recovery costs are rising — in 2023, 16 % of businesses were impacted (21 % in 2019, 18 % in 2021), 30 % of large businesses, scams and fraud 50 % (the most common method), identity theft 31 %, ransomware 13 % (88 % did not pay), 13 % reported to the police, 26 % had a written policy, 22 % had cyber risk insurance, recovery spending about 1.2 billion dollars (double 2021), and the most common activity was monitoring of network and business systems, 46 % of businesses (the survey covers enterprises with 10 employees or more); (3) the organization holds information that belongs to other people — Law 25 defines the confidentiality incident, requires a register of incidents, and requires notification of the CAI and of the persons concerned when there is a risk of serious injury; penalties reach 10 million dollars or 2 % of worldwide turnover (administrative) and 25 million dollars or 4 % (penal); at the federal level the Office of the Privacy Commissioner of Canada applies PIPEDA (Personal Information Protection and Electronic Documents Act); (4) clients, insurers and partners ask for proof; (5) the threat is constant and does not choose by size — the National Cyber Threat Assessment 2025-2026 names ransomware the top cybercrime threat to critical infrastructure, and the Baseline cyber security controls for small and medium organizations start by deciding which systems are in scope and which information has the most value.

              Who is responsible. The owner or management decides how much risk is acceptable and pays for the controls (in Québec the person with the highest authority is by default the person in charge of the protection of personal information); the administrator installs and maintains; every employee applies the rules; the monitoring technician watches the tools, sorts the alerts, analyzes what is abnormal and reports clearly to the people who decide — under supervision, judged on ethics, priorities, communication and confidentiality of the data collected.

              Real-life example 1 — the asset register of Grey Pine. Eight assets A1 to A8; impact 1–5 (what happens if lost, disclosed or altered) and exposure 1–5 (how easily a threat reaches it; exposure stands for likelihood); score = impact × exposure; ≥ 15 high band, 8 to 14 medium, ≤ 7 low. Result: A2 cloud accounting application 5 × 4 = 20; A3 e-mail accounts 4 × 5 = 20; A5 router and firewall RTR01 4 × 4 = 16; A1 file server FS01 5 × 3 = 15; A4 bookkeeper workstations 3 × 4 = 12; A6 backup NAS01 4 × 2 = 8; A7 Wi-Fi AP01 2 × 4 = 8; A8 printer PRN01 1 × 3 = 3. Two observations: the file server has the highest impact but ranks fourth because it is not reachable from the Internet; a score is a help for deciding, not a measurement, so the reason for every rating is written down. The logical diagram shows two items the first register missed: the switch SW01 and three laptops — a first inventory is rarely complete.

              A2.2 Lesson 1.2

              The three security properties

              The six unwanted actions group under three properties, the CIA (Confidentiality, Integrity, Availability) triad, used by the ISO/IEC 27000 family and by FIPS (Federal Information Processing Standards) 199, which calls them the three security objectives.

              Property The question it answers Losing it means Unwanted actions
              Confidentiality Who is able to read this? Unauthorized disclosure access, use, disclosure
              Integrity Is this exact and complete, and was every change authorized? Unauthorized modification or destruction modification, destruction
              Availability Can authorized people use this when they need it? Disruption of access or use disruption, destruction

              Three questions for any alert: was something read, was something changed, was something made unreachable?

              Confidentiality. A loss is often silent (a criminal reads a mailbox for three weeks; nothing changes and nothing stops) — only monitoring reveals it. Controls: authentication (proof of identity; MFA (multi-factor authentication) asks for two proofs of different kinds), authorization and access control with the principle of least privilege, encryption at rest and in transit, administrative controls (classification, training, same-day closure of departing employees' accounts). Privacy is the right of a person to control information about herself (defined by laws such as Law 25); confidentiality is a technical property that applies to any sensitive information. Monitoring observes: failed and successful sign-ins with time and origin, access to sensitive folders, permission changes, new accounts (above all administrator accounts), unusually large outbound transfers.

              Integrity. Exact and complete, changed only by authorized persons in authorized ways; NIST places authenticity and non-repudiation under it. A loss does not require an attacker (an employee overwriting a spreadsheet with an old version). The hash: a hash function takes data of any size and computes a short fixed-size value; SHA-256 (Secure Hash Algorithm, 256-bit) gives 256 bits written as 64 hexadecimal characters. Four properties: deterministic; fixed length; one changed character gives a completely different hash; one-way (the input cannot be rebuilt, and two inputs with the same hash cannot be constructed). Record the hash of the approved file (the baseline); recompute later; equal means not a single byte changed. What a different hash proves: that the content changed after the baseline — not who, when, what or whether it was approved (those answers come from event logs and people). A hash is not encryption: it hides nothing. A tool that recomputes hashes on a schedule and alerts on a difference performs FIM (file integrity monitoring). Other integrity controls: limited write permissions, digital signatures (a hash combined with a secret key), version history, a change management procedure (requested, approved, recorded), backups.

              Availability. Reachable and usable when needed, within an acceptable time; three of the five example failures (full disk, power failure, bad update) involve no attacker — telling security incidents from operational problems is Lesson 1.5. Measures: uptime (99 % allows 87.6 hours of interruption per year, about 3.65 days; 99.9 % allows 8.76 hours; 99.99 % about 53 minutes — the calculation is 8,760 hours × the unavailable fraction); RTO (recovery time objective), the longest acceptable time without a system; RPO (recovery point objective), the largest amount of recent work, expressed as a duration, the organization accepts to lose (an RPO of 24 hours requires at least one backup per day). Controls: tested backups following the 3-2-1 rule (three copies, two kinds of storage, one copy outside the office), a UPS (uninterruptible power supply), duplicate equipment, planned and tested updates, enough capacity, a written plan. Monitoring observes whether devices and services answer, resource use, backup results, certificate and licence validity — most of these signals announce a problem hours or days ahead, which is preventative monitoring in its simplest form.

              Working with the three together. One incident can touch several properties (a stolen unencrypted laptop: confidentiality and availability; ransomware that first copies the files: all three). The properties compete (each extra proof of identity protects confidentiality and slows legitimate users; a shared password destroys confidentiality and the ability to know who did what). Rating the impact (FIPS 199): for each asset, three separate questions, each answered low / moderate / high; the overall level is the highest of the three — the high-water mark rule. Table 8 links each property to the question the technician asks, what tools observe, and an example alert rule ("more than five failed sign-ins on one account in one minute"; "the hash of a protected file differs from its baseline"; "disk used above 90 %; last backup failed").

              Real-life example 2 — one payroll file, three checks. On September 15 the owner approves payroll_2026-09.csv; the technician restricts the permissions to the owner and the payroll group and records the SHA-256 hash (the baseline). On September 17 two of the three checks fail: every user can now read the file, and the hash differs — a fourth row, an unknown payee, 9,999 dollars. The technician does not delete the row and does not restore the permissions on his own: he records the evidence (both hashes, both permission values, the time), informs the owner immediately and keeps the file as it is. Correcting silently destroys the evidence and hides a possible fraud; the Code of Ethics (Legal Notice section 9) requires reporting findings accurately and completely and never concealing an incident.

              A2.3 Lesson 1.3

              The lab environment: VirtualBox, VMware Workstation Pro, the cloud lab and CyberQuébec

              Why a separate lab: a legal reason (observing a system or capturing traffic is lawful only on systems you own or are authorized in writing to work on; a capture on a shared network records other people's communications — sections 6.1 and 7.2), a technical reason (an exercise can fill a disk or make a system unusable; a damaged lab machine is rebuilt in minutes), a teaching reason (identical machines make results comparable). Inside the Authorized Lab Environment you work only on the Designated Targets named by the lab guide: a machine does not become a target because it can be reached.

              How virtualization works: software divides the resources of one physical computer among several isolated environments; virtual disk (a large file on the host that the guest sees as a complete disk), installation image (.iso, downloaded only from the publisher's official site and verified with SHA-256 — the integrity check of Lesson 1.2 applied to your own downloads), snapshot (a recorded state; not a backup, because it lives on the same disk as the machine), clone (an independent copy with its own name; install one clean Linux machine and clone it for each role). Two facts about the host: the processor must allow virtualization (Intel VT-x, AMD-V; switched on in the UEFI/BIOS settings; Windows Task Manager, Performance tab, shows the state — see Enable virtualization on Windows); resources are shared, not created (three machines with 4, 2 and 4 GB use 10 GB; the host needs the rest). Class 2 requirements: 8 GB memory minimum / 16 GB recommended; 4 cores / 6 or more; hardware virtualization enabled; 80 GB / 100 GB or more on a solid-state drive; one hypervisor.

              Network modes (Class 2 table, with VMware names): NAT (VMnet8) — Internet through the host's address, nobody from outside, two VirtualBox machines in this mode do not see each other, used only briefly for updates; bridged (VMnet0) — not used, lab traffic would mix with other people's; host-only (VMnet1) — the standard mode for all lab traffic, host and virtual machines only, no Internet (VirtualBox default range 192.168.56.0/24, host takes .1); internal network (VMware: LAN segment) — virtual machines only, not even the host, for the strictest isolation. Promiscuous mode: the card accepts every frame that reaches it; capture tools switch it on; on a host-only network it sees only lab traffic, on a bridged adapter it records other people's communications (section 184).

              The four environments of the program: (1) VirtualBox — type 2 hypervisor by Oracle, free and open source, current series 7.2; the Extension Pack has its own licence, the PUEL (Personal Use and Evaluation License), and is not needed; download from the official page and compare the SHA-256; default choice for Windows and Linux hosts. (2) VMware Workstation Pro — type 2, Windows and Linux (Fusion Pro for macOS); Broadcom made both free for personal, educational and commercial use in November 2024; a free Broadcom support portal account is needed for the download; versions named by year and half-year (25H2); no publisher support; install one hypervisor, and never run virtual machines in both at once. (3) AWS (Amazon Web Services) Academy Learner Lab — a temporary cloud account by invitation, no credit card; a fixed budget of credits (when spent, the account closes and its content is lost); sessions of four hours (Start Lab / End Lab; running EC2 (Elastic Compute Cloud) instances stop between sessions, work is kept); only some services and two regions; the shared responsibility model (the provider secures buildings, hardware and hypervisor; the customer secures the operating system, accounts, network rules and data — monitoring is the customer's part). It replaces the local lab for a student whose computer fails the readiness check and shows how cloud resources are monitored. (4) CyberQuébec — a CCTT (centre collégial de transfert de technologie) in cybersecurity affiliated with the Cégep de l'Outaouais in Gatineau; it operates a cloud-based laboratory with a cyber range; access for this cohort is not open yet. Mac computers with an Apple processor run only guests built for that processor type: tell the instructor; the cloud lab is usually the simpler path.

              The rules of a safe lab (sections 6.4, 6.6, 6.7, 7.2): isolate; snapshot and back up; use only the designated targets; keep it fictional; use official sources and valid licences (verify the checksum; no cracked copies); respect College equipment and cloud terms; clean up. The most likely mistake in this course: running a capture on the home or campus Wi-Fi "to have real traffic to analyze" — that traffic belongs to other people (section 7.2 and Annex E).

              The planned layout: three virtual machines on one host-only network — monitor01 (Linux, receives the monitoring tool in Lab 2), server01 (Linux server, monitored), desk01 (workstation, monitored); with a 16 GB host, 4, 2 and 4 GB; with an 8 GB host, two machines at a time at 2 GB each. Real-life example 3 — the readiness check in PowerShell (deliverable D3): installed memory ≥ 8 GB, ≥ 4 cores, hardware virtualization enabled, ≥ 80 GB free on drive C:, at least one hypervisor installed; a last informational line reports whether Windows already runs its own hypervisor (Hyper-V), which slows VirtualBox and VMware but does not stop them. A NOT READY verdict is reported to the instructor by MIO before Lab 1.

              Lab 1 in summary (Class 2 version): Friday, September 25, 5 %, Part 1 of the Integrative Project, closes Topic 2, covers element 2 (analyze the topology). It installs no tool and captures no traffic: an analysis on paper whose quality decides everything that follows.

              A3. Class 3

              Common Types of Cyberattacks and Basic Cyber Defense Concepts (Friday, September 18, 2026)

              Fictional organization of this class: Trois-Érables Accounting, twelve people in Montréal; file server TE-FS01 at 192.168.56.10; firewall TE-FW01 (192.168.56.1); access point TE-AP01; switch TE-SW01; workstations WS01 to WS10 (192.168.56.21 to .30); monitoring station TE-MON01 (192.168.56.50, added in Lab 2). The two external attack sources, 203.0.113.45 and 198.51.100.77, belong to blocks reserved for documentation by RFC (Request for Comments) 5737, so they belong to nobody.

              Why a monitoring technician studies attack types: a monitoring tool never displays the word "attack"; it displays events (a failed logon, a new process, a connection to an unknown address, a rise in traffic). A technician who knows the attack types knows what to look for and where. This is performance criterion 1.2 (precise differentiation between types of cyberattacks); Lesson 1.4 covers criterion 1.3 (appropriate illustration of cyber defense concepts).

              A3.1 Lesson 1.3

              Common types of cyberattacks

              Six terms to use with precision (reference: An introduction to the cyber threat environment, Canadian Centre for Cyber Security): a vulnerability is a weakness in a system, a configuration or a human procedure that can be used to cause harm; a threat is any circumstance or event that can cause harm by using a vulnerability; a threat actor is the person or group behind a threat; a cyberattack is a deliberate action by a threat actor against confidentiality, integrity or availability (a disk failure harms availability but is an accident, not an attack); an attack vector is the path used to reach the target (an e-mail, a web form, a remote logon service, a USB (Universal Serial Bus) key, a stolen laptop); the attack surface is the total of all points where an attacker can try to enter — every new Internet-reachable service enlarges it, and the list of things you must monitor.

              Eight attack types, the property each harms, and what monitoring can observe (Table 1, the attack recognition sheet):

              Attack type In one sentence Main property harmed Trace monitoring can observe Data source
              1. Reconnaissance (network scanning) Collecting information about the target before an attack None directly — earliest warning sign One external source tries many ports or many addresses within seconds Firewall log
              2. Social engineering, phishing, spear phishing A fraudulent message imitating a trusted sender to obtain a password or deliver malware; spear phishing is written for one specific person Confidentiality A domain name one letter away from a real partner's; later a logon from a country where the company has no employee Mail service log and quarantine; server security log
              3. Malware: virus, worm, trojan, spyware, keylogger Software written to harm a system or its user (a virus attaches to a file; a worm copies itself over the network without user action; a trojan hides a harmful function in a useful program; spyware records what the user does; a keylogger records keys pressed) Confidentiality, then integrity Antivirus alert; unknown process; connection from a workstation to an unknown external address Workstation antivirus and process events; firewall log
              3b. Ransomware Encrypts the victim's files and demands payment; often copies the files first Availability, often confidentiality One account modifies hundreds of files in minutes; files receive a new unknown extension; shortly before, an antivirus alert File audit on the server
              4. Password attacks Brute force: very many passwords against one account; dictionary: only probable words; password spraying: one or two common passwords against many accounts, so no account reaches the lockout limit; credential stuffing: pairs stolen from another website Confidentiality Series of Windows events 4625 (failed logon); 4740 (account locked out) for brute force; failures on many accounts from one source, then a 4624 (successful logon), for spraying Server security log
              5. Denial of service (DoS) and distributed denial of service (DDoS) More requests than the service can process, or requests built to make it fail; DDoS uses thousands of infected computers controlled as a botnet Availability Traffic far above normal; very many source addresses; response time rising until the service stops Firewall log and traffic counters
              6. On-path attack (older name MITM, Man-in-the-Middle) A device placed between two parties reads or modifies their traffic; ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) spoofing sends false address announcements; a rogue access point uses the office network name Confidentiality and integrity One IP (Internet Protocol) address associated with two hardware addresses; an access point with the office name absent from the inventory Switch address table and wireless survey
              7. Injection (SQL (Structured Query Language) injection) A fragment of database command typed in a form field and executed by the database Confidentiality and integrity Requests with database keywords or unusual punctuation in a field; rise in database errors Web server and database logs
              8. Insider misuse Authorized access used for an unauthorized purpose (employee, former employee, contractor) — no technical barrier is broken, so prevention cannot stop it Confidentiality, sometimes integrity and availability Access to many files outside normal duties; unusual hours; large copies to removable media or personal cloud storage File audit on the server

              Two more terms: a zero-day attack uses a vulnerability the publisher does not know or has not corrected — no update exists on the day of the attack; a supply-chain attack reaches the target through a supplier (a modified update, a compromised provider). In both, the preventive controls are intact and the attack still succeeds — the main argument of Lesson 1.4. Ransomware is named the top cybercrime threat to Canada's critical infrastructure in the National Cyber Threat Assessment 2025-2026.

              Windows event identifiers to know (Table 3): 4624 an account was successfully logged on (normal in large numbers; suspicious after many failures from the same source or at an unusual hour or place); 4625 an account failed to log on (every password attack produces it; count per account and per source); 4740 a user account was locked out (proof that the lockout policy, a preventive control, reacted); 4720 a user account was created; 4732 a member was added to a security-enabled local group (watch Administrators); 1102 the audit log was cleared (attackers clear logs to remove traces); 7045 a new service was installed (System log; malware installs itself as a service); 4688 a new process was created (only when process-creation auditing is enabled). Official description: Microsoft documentation of event 4625.

              Real-life example 1 — a Friday morning on the file server (September 18, 2026; fifteen records: time, event identifier, account, source). Records 2 and 3: one failure then a success twelve seconds later, same account m.tremblay, same workstation WS01 inside the office — a typing mistake. Records 4 to 9: six failures in ten seconds, always on administrator, always from 203.0.113.45 — no person types that fast: a brute-force attack. Records 10 to 14: five failures from 198.51.100.77, one every thirty seconds, each on a different account (a.gagnon, j.roy, l.cote, m.tremblay, s.nguyen) — password spraying. Record 15: fifteen minutes later, 09:31:05, the same address logs on successfully as j.roy: the attacker found a valid password. Program 1 applies the reasoning with two counters per source address: the number of failures and the number of different accounts. The deliverable is one result line per source (failures, distinct accounts, conclusion); the two recognition rules enter the Lab 1 plan as suspicious behaviours, become alert rules in Lab 2, and are evidence in Lab 3.

              A3.2 Lesson 1.4

              Basic cyber defense concepts: prevention, detection, response

              Three functions, classified by the moment at which they act. Cyber defense is the set of measures an organization uses against cyberattacks; a single measure is a security control. A preventive control acts before the attack succeeds; a detective control acts during the attack or shortly after and makes it visible; a corrective control acts after the incident is confirmed, limits the damage and returns systems to normal. The three moments give prevention, detection and response.

              Seven preventive controls you meet most often: security updates (patches) correct known vulnerabilities; MFA (Multi-Factor Authentication) makes a stolen password insufficient; an account lockout policy blocks an account after a fixed number of failed logons and stops brute force; a firewall allows only authorized connections; least privilege limits what a compromised account or a dishonest insider can reach; offline backups make recovery possible after ransomware; awareness training teaches employees to recognize phishing.

              Why prevention is never sufficient — four reasons: a zero-day has no update; people make errors (one employee in a hundred typing a password on a false page is enough); an insider already holds authorized access; money and staff are limited, so some systems are always less protected. A professional defender assumes some attacks will pass and prepares to see them and act. Seeing them is detection — the subject of this course.

              Detection needs three things: data sources (event logs of servers and workstations, logs of the firewall and other network equipment, captured traffic, alerts of security software); a baseline (a recorded description of normal activity — without it nobody can say an activity is abnormal; built in Lab 2); detection rules — a threshold rule alerts when a count passes a limit within a period ("five failed logons from one source in ten minutes"); a signature rule alerts when the data matches the known pattern of a specific attack. Tools that apply the rules: an IDS (Intrusion Detection System) analyzes traffic or host activity and raises alerts; an IPS (Intrusion Prevention System) does the same and can also block, which makes it a preventive control as well; a SIEM (Security Information and Event Management) platform collects the logs of many systems in one place, relates events from different sources and raises alerts; the people who read them work in a SOC (Security Operations Centre). Thousands of events produce tens of alerts, and a few alerts become incidents. False positive (an alert for legitimate activity — the accountant who forgot her password on Monday), false negative (a real attack with no alert); a threshold too low buries the technicians in false positives until they stop reading, too high lets attacks pass; adjusting the rules to reduce both errors is tuning (Topic 6). Speed of detection: MTTD (Mean Time to Detect).

              Response — five steps, under supervision (reference: the NIST incident response project, publication SP (Special Publication) 800-61, revised in 2025): preparation (a plan, named responsible people, current contact information — before any incident); analysis (verify the alert, determine what happened and which systems are affected); containment (limit the damage: disable a compromised account, isolate an infected workstation); eradication and recovery (remove the cause, restore from backups, return to normal); lessons learned (record what happened, improve the controls). Speed of response: MTTR (Mean Time to Respond), from detection to the end of recovery. Your part: the competency says you work under supervision — the technician detects, analyzes, documents and reports; the technician does not decide alone to block an address, disable an account or shut down a server on a production network, because a containment action changes the system and can interrupt legitimate users; it needs the approval of the person responsible (Legal Notice section 7.4 gives the same rule for laboratory work). Your most valuable product is a clear incident note: what was observed, when, on which system, from which source, and what you recommend. In Québec: an incident involving personal information is a confidentiality incident under the Act as amended by Law 25; the organization records it in a register and, if there is a risk of serious injury, notifies the CAI and the persons concerned — that decision belongs to the person responsible for the protection of personal information, not to the technician, who makes it possible with an accurate, fast note. Worked case of all three functions: the Ransomware playbook of the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security.

              Defense in depth: several independent controls placed one after the other, so that the failure of one does not give access to the information. Frameworks: the NIST CSF (Cybersecurity Framework) 2.0 has six functions — Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover; Protect corresponds to prevention, Detect to detection, Respond and Recover to response; Govern and Identify are the foundation (know the rules, know the network — Topic 2 and Lab 1).

              Real-life example 2 — which defense function reacted? Same fifteen records, in time order. One preventive control: an account is locked after five consecutive failed logons. One detective control: an alert when one source produces five failed logons within ten minutes. At 09:10:09, the fifth failure on administrator arrives: the account locks and the alert fires in the same second — both controls worked. Then the spraying: each account receives one failure only, so the lockout never reacts; the detection rule counts by source, not by account, and fires at 09:16:20, two minutes after the first attempt. At 09:31:05 the attacker logs on as j.roy: the response panel receives a high-priority line because the logon comes from a source already under alert. Between the alert and that logon there are 14 minutes 45 seconds — the time detection gave the office; if nobody reads the alert, detection had no effect. The program recommends four actions and changes nothing: the approval belongs to the supervisor. Table 2, the control map, gives prevention, detection and response for each attack type (for brute force: lockout, long passwords, MFA / five or more failures on one account or from one source within ten minutes / verify the lockout, record the source, recommend blocking it on the firewall; for insider misuse: least privilege, separation of duties, same-day closure of accounts / access outside duties or hours, large copies / preserve the logs, report to the supervisor only).

              What you keep from Class 3 (Table 6): Table 1 (attack recognition sheet) decides what to observe on each asset and in which source (Lab 1), which logs the tool collects (Lab 2), and the attack type that matches an anomaly (Lab 3); Table 2 (control map) gives the expected control per asset, the alert rules, the recommended actions; Table 3 (event identifiers) gives the events to collect, the filters and alert conditions, and the identifiers to quote as evidence; the rules of Program 1 become the first two alerts; the incident note of Program 2 is the format of the Lab 3 report.

              A4. Class 4

              Security Issues versus Performance Issues, and the close of Topic 1 (Saturday, September 19, 2026)

              Fictional organization: Atelier Nord-Ouest, a design and print studio in Montréal with fourteen employees (the case of the whole Integrative Project in Classes 1 and 4): router with firewall RTR01 on a 300/100 Mbps (megabits per second) fibre connection, unmanaged switch SW01, wireless access point AP01, Windows file server FS01 (client projects), Linux backup server BK01, twelve workstations WS01–WS12, large-format plotter PLT01, office printer PRN01. Business hours Monday to Saturday, 8 a.m. to 6 p.m.; backup every night at 01:00; no staff on Sunday.

              A4.1 Subject 1.5

              Security issues versus performance issues (criterion 1.4)

              1.5.1 Five words that must mean the same thing for everyone: an event is any observable occurrence, neutral by itself; an alert is a notification produced when an event or measurement matches a rule or crosses a threshold a human configured in advance — a claim made by a tool, not a fact; an incident is an event or group of connected events that harms or threatens to harm confidentiality, integrity or availability, or breaks a policy — a conclusion reached by a person after looking at evidence; the baseline (reference database of normal activity) is a written, measured description of how a system behaves when nothing is wrong, recorded over a period long enough to include the normal cycles (working hours, evenings, week-ends, month-end) — without it, "high", "slow" and "unusual" have no meaning; a false positive is an alert raised when nothing abnormal happened, a false negative is the absence of an alert when something abnormal did happen — both are failures of the monitoring configuration, both reduced by a good baseline. Order in practice: a tool observes an event, a rule turns some events into an alert, a human decides whether the alert describes an incident. Your work lives in the third step.

              1.5.2 A performance issue is a condition in which a system still behaves exactly as designed but delivers its function too slowly, with less capacity than required, or with interruptions, because of demand, resource limits, faults or configuration; no unauthorized person is involved. Usual causes: demand above planned capacity; exhaustion of CPU (Central Processing Unit) time, RAM (Random Access Memory), disk space, disk input/output or bandwidth; a hardware fault; a change made by the organization itself; a design limit. The evidence is quantitative and repeatable: values rise and fall with the load, follow a schedule or the number of users, or start with a documented change.

              1.5.3 A security issue is a condition caused by, or indicating, an action that was not authorized, an attempt at such an action, or a weakness that makes it possible; it affects at least one of the three properties. The distinguishing element is not severity and not slowness: it is the presence of an actor — a person, a script or a program acting outside its authorization — and the traces an actor leaves that a machine fault never leaves: authentication records that match no legitimate pattern (failures then a success when the office is empty); new accounts, group memberships, permissions, services or scheduled tasks that no change record explains; files created, renamed or encrypted in volume by one account or process; connections to destinations absent from the baseline, especially outbound with volume; records that are missing (cleared logs, gaps, an agent that stopped reporting); software installed without a record, or a hash that no longer matches. The point that decides most cases: a performance issue is explained by demand, faults and change; a security issue is explained by an actor. When you cannot explain a symptom by demand, a fault or a documented change, and traces of an actor are present, the classification is security — even when the service works perfectly.

              1.5.4 Why the two look alike on the first screen. Users report symptoms, not causes (it is slow, it stopped, it is full, it is behaving strangely). Examples: the shared application slow every morning (everyone signs in within ten minutes, or automated password guessing / DDoS — decided by requests per source and the ratio of failed to successful sign-ins); the file server disk filling quickly (a backup job keeping more copies, or ransomware writing encrypted copies — decided by which process writes, which account owns the new files, the extensions, the write rate against the baseline); the Internet link saturated in the evening (updates and video, or exfiltration — direction, destinations, protocol, volume per host); one workstation at full processor load (a runaway application or antivirus scan, or cryptocurrency mining — process name and path, digital signature, persistence entries, outbound destinations); a service restarting repeatedly (a defective driver or memory leak, or an actor crashing it — who issued the restart, sign-in records, configuration modification times). Two examinable facts: a security incident can produce a performance symptom (encryption of a share, DoS, mining all consume resources; the slowness is real but is not the cause); a security incident can produce no performance symptom at all (copying a client folder to a personal cloud, creating a hidden administrator account) — which is why monitoring cannot be limited to performance counters.

              1.5.5 The four-question triage (asked in the same sequence every time, each answered with data you can point at):

              # Question Where the answer comes from What it establishes
              1 What exactly is affected, and since when? The report, the asset inventory, the monitoring history, the times in the logs Scope and start time
              2 Does demand or a change explain it? Active users and sessions, scheduled jobs, backup windows, update history, the change record Whether the measurement follows normal work
              3 Is there evidence of an actor? Authentication logs, account and group changes, new services and tasks, process lists, outbound connections, file creation patterns, integrity checks Whether something acted outside its authorization — decides most cases
              4 What does the baseline say? The reference database for this asset, this hour, this day of the week Whether the value is outside the normal range; without it, questions 2 and 3 are guesses

              The decision rule: traces of an actor with no authorization → Security (treat as an incident until the evidence disproves it); no trace of an actor, and demand, a fault or a documented change explains the values, which stay inside the baseline → Performance; traces of an actor and a resource exhausted → Both (security path first; the resource problem is a consequence); the evidence does not answer question 3 → Undetermined (preserve the data, raise the priority, escalate; never close a case as "just slow"). The rule is asymmetric because of the cost of the two mistakes: calling a security incident a performance problem leaves an actor inside the network; calling a performance problem a security incident costs an escalation and some hours.

              1.5.6 What each verdict obliges you to do: Performance — measure, identify the constrained resource, plan a correction, schedule it as a change; inform the service owner and operations; record as a service request. Security — preserve the evidence before changing anything (export the logs, note exact times, do not reboot, do not delete, do not "clean"), then follow the incident procedure; inform the person named in it; in Québec, where personal information is involved, record the confidentiality incident in the register and, where there is a risk of serious injury, notify the CAI and the persons concerned. Both — security procedure first, keep the performance measurements as evidence of impact; both audiences with one single timeline of facts. Undetermined — preserve, widen the collection, set a temporary alert and a review time; inform your supervisor with a written statement of what is missing and what you propose to collect. Two obligations from section 7.2 apply throughout: capture only on systems you own or the lab guide designates; treat every capture, log and baseline as personal information — keep the minimum, store it in the lab, delete it when marked.

              1.5.7 Five mistakes beginners make: deciding from the severity of the symptom (severity measures impact, not origin — decide from question 3); rebooting or reimaging first (destroys memory contents, process lists and temporary files — export first, act second); comparing against a feeling instead of a baseline ("that looks high" is not a measurement); treating one alert as one incident (incidents are built from several sources that agree); closing an unexplained case ("it went away" is not a diagnosis — it becomes Undetermined with a review date).

              Real-life example — two reports on the same week-end. Report A, Saturday 13:10: sending a quote to the plotter takes forty seconds instead of four, Saturday afternoons only; on FS01, processor 60–75 % and disk writing 40–60 MB/s (megabytes per second) from 13:00 to 15:00 every Saturday for five weeks; no failed sign-ins above the usual two or three; no new accounts or services; the archive job to BK01 was moved to Saturday 13:00 in the change record of August 15. Answers: one server, Saturdays, five weeks / yes, a documented change and a scheduled job / no actor / inside the Saturday baseline → Performance; the correction is a scheduling decision with the service owner. Report B, Sunday 09:20: two users locked out, the server slow during the night, files with a strange extension; between 01:40 and 02:35, 412 failed sign-ins for three accounts from one address, then one successful sign-in at 02:05; processor 96 %; disk writing 180 MB/s; 1,940 files created with an extension absent from the baseline; one outbound connection to a never-seen address; the Windows security log cleared at 02:31. Answers: the file server, Sunday night, fifty-five minutes / no job at that time, nobody works Sunday / yes — lockouts, success after failures, mass file creation, new destination, cleared log / far outside the Sunday baseline → Security that also produces a performance symptom, reported as Both: security procedure first, processor and disk figures kept as evidence of impact; client files involved, so the incident goes in the register of confidentiality incidents. Do not restart FS01, do not delete the new files, do not run a cleaning tool; export the security log, the file listing with times and the firewall connection record first — the cleared log at 02:31 is itself evidence: an action, and actions have authors. The completed triage sheet becomes Appendix A of the Lab 1 plan; the proposed threshold becomes an alert value in Lab 2; the same sheet is the reporting form for Lab 3.

              A4.2 Recap of Topic 1

              Foundations of cybersecurity

              • 1.1 Cybersecurity is a property of how an organization works, not a product or a department. Four reasons organizations need it: operational, financial, legal (Law 25: protect personal information, keep a register of confidentiality incidents, notify the CAI and the persons concerned when there is a risk of serious injury), reputational. Monitoring is the part of cybersecurity that makes the other parts visible.
              • 1.2 The three properties define what "protected" means; the first line of every incident report says which property is at risk. They are not ranked: for the client project folder, confidentiality and integrity dominate; for the plotter queue on a delivery day, availability dominates.
              • 1.3 You are not asked to perform attacks; you are asked to recognize the trace each one leaves. The recap table adds "malicious update or supplier compromise" (integrity; a signed component behaving in a new way, new outbound destinations after an update, changes with no matching change record) and lists phishing (confidentiality), malware including ransomware (integrity, then availability), DoS/DDoS (availability), password attacks (confidentiality), interception/on-path (confidentiality, integrity), insider misuse (confidentiality).
              • 1.4 Controls by moment: prevention (authentication including MFA, permissions, firewall rules, segmentation, updates, hardening, training), detection (logging, monitoring tools, IDS, SIEM, file integrity checking, alerting on a baseline deviation), response (isolating a host, disabling an account, blocking an address, restoring from backup, the incident procedure). Controls by nature: technical (a firewall rule), administrative or managerial (a policy, an access review), operational (a procedure carried out by people, such as log review), physical (a lock on the server cabinet). Defense in depth. The sentence for the examination: detection exists because prevention fails.
              • 1.5 Performance is explained by demand, a fault or a documented change; security by an actor. Four questions, four verdicts.

              How Topic 1 is assessed (element 1 criteria): 1.1 correct identification of issues linked to confidentiality, integrity and availability (subject 1.2 — impact column of the Lab 1 plan); 1.2 precise differentiation between types of cyberattacks (subject 1.3 — threat column); 1.3 appropriate illustration of cyber defence concepts (subject 1.4 — control column); 1.4 clear distinction between performance and security issues (subject 1.5 — triage sheet of Lab 1 and anomaly report of Lab 3). All four are examined in Quiz 1 and in the mid-term.

              Real-life example — turning Topic 1 into the monitoring priority list of Atelier Nord-Ouest. For each of the eight assets: the property that matters most, the most likely attack, and a priority from impact (1–3) × exposure (1–3): impact 3 if work stops or client information is exposed, 2 if work is slowed, 1 if minor; exposure 3 if reachable from the Internet or an untrusted network, 2 if every internal user reaches it daily, 1 if access is restricted. Tier 1 = score 6 or more, Tier 2 = 3 to 5, Tier 3 = 2 or less. Result: RTR01 3 × 3 = 9 (availability then integrity; denial of service, exploitation of an exposed service); FS01 3 × 2 = 6 (confidentiality and integrity; ransomware, insider misuse); AP01 2 × 3 = 6 (confidentiality; unauthorized association, interception) — Tier 1; WS01–WS12 2 × 2 = 4 (integrity; phishing leading to malware); BK01 3 × 1 = 3 (integrity and availability; ransomware reaching the backups) — Tier 2; PLT01 2 × 1 = 2; PRN01 1 × 2 = 2; SW01 2 × 1 = 2 — Tier 3. The inventory file uses the words High, Medium and Low, which the script converts to 3, 2 and 1; the rule is written down so the ranking can be defended in front of the owner — what criterion 2.3 asks in Topic 2. Tier 1 assets are the ones instrumented in Lab 2 and analyzed in Lab 3.

              Quiz 1 (5 %) was written at the end of Class 4, online, covering subjects 1.1 to 1.5 in their entirety. Suggested revision order: the Topic 1 diagram, the five definitions of 1.5.1, the attack table of the recap, the four triage questions.

              A5. Class 5

              Topic 2: Understanding the Network to Be Monitored, Lessons 2.1 and 2.2 (Monday, September 21, 2026)

              Fictional organization of this class: the Fictiva Dental Clinic (two dentists, a hygienist, a receptionist, an office manager); staff network 192.168.10.0/24, guest Wi-Fi 192.168.50.0/24; twelve devices: MODEM-ISP-01 (bridge mode), FW-EDGE-01 (192.168.10.1, default gateway, gives out addresses), SW-CORE-01 (.2, 24-port managed switch), AP-FRONT-01 (.3, staff and guest Wi-Fi), SRV-FILES-01 (.10), NAS-BACKUP-01 (.11), WS-RECEP-01 (.21), WS-DENT-01 (.22), WS-XRAY-01 (.24), LT-ADMIN-01 (.31), PRN-FRONT-01 (.40), CAM-DOOR-01 (.41).

              A5.1 Lesson 2.1

              Network components: servers, workstations, network equipment

              What a network is made of. A computer network is a set of devices, called nodes, connected by links (cable or radio) so they can exchange data; a node with its own address that runs programs sending or receiving data is a host. From a monitoring point of view every node is an asset. The asset inventory records at least the hostname, address, role, location, owner and dependent devices. The inventory comes first because a monitoring tool watches only the devices it has been told about: a device missing from the inventory is not monitored. This is why the first of the CIS Critical Security Controls is Inventory and Control of Enterprise Assets, why the NIST Cybersecurity Framework places asset management (category ID.AM (Identify function, Asset Management category)) at the start of its Identify function, and why the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security baseline controls ask organizations to identify systems and information before choosing protections.

              Four families, decided by what a device does, not what it looks like: servers provide services to other devices, nobody works on them directly (file server, backup storage); workstations are endpoints used directly by one person with a full operating system (reception desktop, office laptop); network equipment forwards traffic that belongs to other devices (switch, firewall, access point, modem); other endpoints are fixed-function devices that run firmware only (printer, entrance camera). An ordinary desktop sharing the patient database with eight colleagues is doing the work of a server.

              Servers. A server provides a service to other computers over the network; the users of the service are its clients (the client-server model). A service runs continuously and waits for requests on a numbered port of the server's address — a web service normally waits on port 443 of the TCP (Transmission Control Protocol), the protocol that delivers data reliably between two hosts. Common roles: file server; database server; DNS (Domain Name System) server (translates names into addresses); DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol) server (gives an address to each device that joins; in a small office this often runs on the firewall); backup server or NAS (Network-Attached Storage); web and e-mail servers. Server hardware runs 24 hours a day: ECC (Error-Correcting Code) memory, disks combined with RAID (Redundant Array of Independent Disks), two power supplies, a separate remote management interface; many servers are virtual machines, so the physical host becomes a single point of failure for all of them. Monitoring data on servers: whether each service answers; processor, memory and disk use; successful and failed logons and account changes in the event logs; the result of every backup. Server versus workstation (Table 2.1-1): server edition versus desktop edition operating system; 24/7 versus working hours; risks: service outage, data theft, ransomware on shared data versus phishing, malicious downloads, lost or stolen laptop.

              Workstations and other endpoints. An endpoint is a device at the edge of the network where data is created or used, as opposed to equipment that carries it. Workstations run a general-purpose OS (Operating System) and are where people act (attachments, websites, USB keys), so they are the usual starting point of phishing and malware; laptops leave the building. Monitoring data: security event logs (logons, failed logons, new software, account changes), endpoint protection alerts, update level. Other endpoints — printers, scanners, IP cameras, door controllers, sensors, smart televisions and other IoT (Internet of Things) devices — run firmware, are easy to forget, rarely updated, often on factory settings, and must appear in the inventory like any computer; monitoring data: reachability, firmware version, unexpected connections (a printer that suddenly sends data to the Internet). A camera that records people and a workstation storing patient images hold personal information protected by the Act (Law 25), supervised by the CAI — which is why the priority calculation of the example adds points to such devices.

              Network equipment and the OSI (Open Systems Interconnection) model (seven layers; three are enough here): layer 1 physical (signals on cable or radio); layer 2 data link (frames delivered inside one local network using MAC (Media Access Control) addresses, the hardware address of each network interface); layer 3 network (packets delivered between networks using IP (Internet Protocol) addresses). The NIC (Network Interface Card) connects a node to the medium and has its own MAC address. A switch connects the devices of one LAN (Local Area Network); it learns which MAC address is reached through which port by reading the source address of every frame, stores the pairs in its MAC address table, forwards each frame only to the port of its destination, and sends a frame for an unknown address to all ports; a managed switch can be configured and monitored remotely and can send a copy of the traffic of chosen ports to another port — port mirroring, also called SPAN (Switched Port Analyzer) — which is how the monitoring sensor of Lab 2 receives traffic; the older hub repeated every signal to all ports and is no longer installed. A router connects different networks (the LAN and the provider's network, part of a WAN (Wide Area Network)), reads the destination IP address and chooses an interface from its routing table; its interface inside a network is that network's default gateway. A firewall allows or blocks traffic by rules on sources, destinations, ports and applications, records its decisions in logs, sits at the boundary between a trusted and an untrusted network, and in small offices also routes and performs NAT (Network Address Translation) of private addresses into the single public address. A wireless access point (AP) connects Wi-Fi devices (IEEE (Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers) 802.11) to the wired Ethernet network (IEEE 802.3) and can broadcast several network names, each an SSID (Service Set Identifier). A modem converts the provider's line into Ethernet, in bridge mode passes traffic without routing, and normally belongs to the provider. A SOHO (Small Office/Home Office) router combines router, firewall, switch, access point and DHCP server in one box: document each function separately, because each needs its own monitoring. Every packet between two hosts crosses at least one piece of network equipment: if a switch or firewall fails, every device behind it loses its connection (availability), and the same devices are the best places to observe traffic. They are monitored with SNMP (Simple Network Management Protocol) (status and counters), the logs they send to a log server (syslog), and copies of their traffic.
