              Class 4, Atelier Nord-Ouest priority list Impact 1–3 × exposure 1–3 (words High/Medium/Low converted to 3/2/1) score = impact × exposure Tier 1 ≥ 6; Tier 2 3–5; Tier 3 ≤ 2
              Class 5, Fictiva inventory Points: dependents ≥ 4 → +4, 1–3 → +2; personal information +2; Internet-facing +2; interactive user +1 sum of points ≥ 4 High; 2–3 Medium; 0–1 Low
              Class 7, Val-des-Pins Criticality 1–3 (high-water mark of C/I/A impacts) × exposure 1–3 (from E1–E5: 0–1 → 1, 2–3 → 2, 4–5 → 3) score = criticality × exposure (1–9) High 6–9 (Tier 1); Moderate 3–4 (Tier 2); Low 1–2 (Tier 3)
              A8.3

              Numbers and dates worth memorizing

              • Course: 75 hours, 2-3-1, 2 2/3 credits; 19 classes, Sept 14 – Oct 19, 2026; no class Oct 5 and Oct 12.
              • Marks: quizzes 4 × 5 % (Sept 19, 26, Oct 10, 15); labs 3 × 5 % (Sept 25, Oct 3, Oct 16); mid-term 25 % (Oct 1); final 40 % (Oct 19); 60 % on the final and 60 % overall; late work −10 % per day, nothing after 7 days; up to −10 % for literacy; medical certificate above 5 days.
              • Baseline: μ + 3σ ≈ 99.7 %; 168 hourly counts in one week.
              • Uptime: 99 % = 87.6 h/year; 99.9 % = 8.76 h; 99.99 % ≈ 53 min. Backups 3-2-1.
              • SHA-256: 256 bits, 64 hexadecimal characters.
              • Windows events: 4624 success, 4625 failure, 4740 lockout, 4720 account created, 4732 group member added, 1102 audit log cleared, 7045 new service, 4688 new process.
              • Class 3 example: lockout after 5 consecutive failures; alert at 5 failures from one source in 10 minutes; lockout and alert 09:10:09; spraying alert 09:16:20; attacker logon 09:31:05; 14 min 45 s.
              • Class 4 report B: 412 failed sign-ins, success at 02:05, 96 % processor, 180 MB/s, 1,940 files, log cleared 02:31.
              • Statistics Canada 2023: 16 % impacted (1 in 6), 30 % of large businesses, 50 % scams and fraud, 13 % ransomware (88 % did not pay), 46 % monitor, ~1.2 billion dollars recovery.
              • Law 25 penalties: 10 M$ or 2 % (administrative), 25 M$ or 4 % (penal). Criminal Code: s. 342.1, 342.2, 430(1.1), 184. CASL s. 8.
              • Ports: web 443 TCP; syslog UDP 514; SNMP UDP 161 and 162. /24 = 256 addresses, 254 usable. RFC 1918 private; RFC 5737 documentation.
              • Lab hosts: 8 GB / 16 GB RAM; 80 GB / 100–120 GB disk; 4 / 6 cores; VirtualBox host-only default 192.168.56.0/24.
              • Val-des-Pins: CAD 1,500; 6 h/month (1.5 h reserve → 4.5 h); 1.2 TB free on NAS-01; 5 Mbit/s ceiling; 90-day retention; 4-minute clock drift; storage formula 25 events/s × 300 B × 86,400 × 90 ≈ 58 GB; envelope 2,275 MB and 60 min per day; wish list 9,165 MB and 110 min; 27 needs, 24 covered, 3 gaps; result 1,875 MB (82 %) and 60 min (100 %); four deferred, one reduced, one override; review date Oct 16.
              PART B

              Ten case studies with their most probable answers

              Work each case in three steps: name the lesson it belongs to, write your answer in three to five lines, then compare with the model answer. In the examination, a case question is graded on the reasoning shown, not on the verdict alone.

              Case study 1

              Reading the outline as a specification (Class 1, Lessons 1.1 and 1.2)

              Situation. Three students compare notes after Class 1. Student A: "The course is 75 hours, so it is mostly lectures — I will revise at the end." Student B: "I had 88 % before the final and I am sure I can pass the course with 52 % on the final exam, because the average is 73 %." Student C has written a monitoring scope register for Atelier Nord-Ouest that lists the router, the file server, the switch and the ten workstations, with elements 1, 2, 3 and 4 of EZ01 demonstrated, and asks whether it is complete.

              Questions. (a) What does the ponderation 2-3-1 tell Student A, and why is "revising at the end" the wrong plan for this course? (b) What grade does Student B actually receive, and which two rules decide it? (c) What is missing from Student C's register, and how would the program of Applied example 1.1 report it?

              Model answer. (a) 2-3-1 means two hours of theory, three hours of laboratory or practical work and one hour of personal study per week; the course is weighted towards practical work, not lectures. The format is intensive — 75 hours in six weeks — and the quizzes are cumulative, so the gap between meeting a concept and being examined on it is measured in days; Quiz 1 falls on the fourth class and the mid-term on the tenth. Retrieval practice spaced over the weeks is the plan the schedule is built for. (b) Student B fails the course with a recorded grade of 52 %. Rule 1: at least 60 % on the final examination is required, and a final below 60 % makes the recorded course grade equal to that examination grade — the weighted average of 73 % is never computed. Rule 2 (60 % overall) would also have to hold. (c) Element 5, optimizing surveillance tools, is not demonstrated by any asset in the register, so the competency is not covered in full; the register also omits the backup server, the two access points, the printer and the camera recorder from the studio's inventory. The program ez01_scope_register.py subtracts the set of covered elements from the full set of five and prints the remainder as a gap — element 5 in this case — so that the gap is found on paper on day one instead of at the end of Lab 3. The backup server (service status baseline plus tuning note) and the camera recorder (data-handling note) are the assets that would demonstrate element 5.

              Case study 2

              A baseline of failed logons (Class 1, Lesson 1.3)

              Situation. For one week (168 hourly counts) the failed-logon events of the Atelier Nord-Ouest file server give a mean μ of 4.0 per hour and a standard deviation σ of 2.0. On the day of live observation the hourly counts are: 3, 5, 2, 11, 4, 0, 6, 27 (the last hour being 03:00 to 04:00 on a Sunday). A colleague proposes to replace the whole method with the rule "alert on any failed logon".

              Questions. (a) What is the detection threshold at μ + 3σ, and which hours are flagged? (b) Which of the flagged hours would you triage first, and what would you check? (c) Why is the colleague's rule useless, and what does the pipeline call the stage that produced the hourly counts?

              Model answer. (a) μ + 3σ = 4.0 + 3 × 2.0 = 10.0. Hours above the line: the fourth hour (11) and the eighth hour (27). Roughly 99.7 % of normal observations fall within three standard deviations of the mean for an approximately normal distribution, so values above 10 are rare enough to deserve a human's attention. (b) The hour with 27 failures at 03:00 on a Sunday is triaged first: it is far above the line and it happens when the studio has nobody at work (no staff on Sunday). The check is whether the flagged failures share a source address or an account: many failures on one account from one source suggests brute force; failures spread over many accounts from one source suggests password spraying; a success (event 4624) from the same source after the failures raises the priority. The hour with 11 failures at a working hour could be a mistyped password on a phone that retries, which is exactly the kind of harmless noise the baseline is meant to absorb. (c) Failed authentications are noisy in a harmless way — staff mistype passwords, phones hold old credentials, scheduled tasks run with expired accounts — so "alert on any failed logon" fires all day and produces alert fatigue, after which genuine alerts are dismissed by habit; the count per hour compared with its own history is informative where the raw event is not. Grouping the events into hourly counts on a synchronized clock is the normalize stage of the pipeline (collect → normalize → baseline → detect → triage → diagnose → report and optimize); the threshold is chosen in the baseline stage and applied in the detect stage. Also note that a baseline built from a Tuesday afternoon would alarm every Monday morning, and that the baseline must be rebuilt when the network legitimately changes (criterion 5.1).

              Case study 3

              The pre-flight check finds a bridged adapter (Class 1, Lesson 1.4; Class 2, Lesson 1.3)

              Situation. Before Lab 1 a student runs the pre-flight script. It reports: AN-FS01 — adapter 1 internal atelier-lan, snapshot present; AN-BK01 — adapter 1 internal atelier-lan, snapshot present; AN-MON01 — adapter 1 internal atelier-lan, adapter 2 bridged, snapshot present; free space 95 GB; verdict FAIL. The student says: "It is only the monitoring station, I used the bridged adapter last night to download packages, and everything else passes — the report should say conformity."

              Questions. (a) Which of the three conditions of an Authorized Lab Environment is broken, and why does one adapter fail the whole report? (b) What could have happened if the student had started a packet capture on AN-MON01 in that state, and which law is concerned? (c) What should the adapter have been set to for the download, and what is the correct configuration for AN-MON01?

              Model answer. (a) Condition 2 — the environment must be disconnected from, or securely segregated from, any production, institutional, corporate, public or third-party network. A bridged adapter places the virtual machine directly on the student's home or campus network, as if it were another physical computer. The check is designed to give a specific, actionable failure rather than a reassuring summary: a single bridged adapter is enough to turn the laboratory into a shared network, so the verdict cannot be conformity while it exists. Nothing on the screen would otherwise tell the student. (b) A capture tool switches the network card to promiscuous mode, which accepts every frame that reaches it; on a bridged adapter connected to a shared network the capture records the communications of the household or the campus. That can constitute interception of a private communication under section 184 of the Criminal Code, and it breaks sections 6.4 and 7.2 of the Acceptable Use Policy ("never enable promiscuous or monitor mode on a network you share with other people"). The Class 2 handout calls this the most likely mistake in the course. (c) Updates are downloaded through a NAT (Network Address Translation) adapter, connected only for the time of the update and then disconnected; NAT allows no inbound connection from outside and, in VirtualBox, two machines in NAT mode do not even see each other. AN-MON01 is configured with the internal network atelier-lan for the laboratory traffic plus a host-only adapter so that the monitoring console can be reached from the host's browser; neither of these reaches the outside world. After correcting the adapter, the student re-runs the check and attaches the dated conformity report (deliverable D4) to the submission.

              Case study 4

              The risk register of Grey Pine (Class 2, Lesson 1.1)

              Situation. The owner of Grey Pine Bookkeeping asks why the e-mail accounts are ranked above the file server "when the file server holds everything". The technician's register gives: file server FS01 impact 5, exposure 3; e-mail accounts impact 4, exposure 5; backup NAS01 impact 4, exposure 2; printer impact 1, exposure 3. A new item is found during the walk-through: a Wi-Fi access point used by staff phones and by visiting clients, reachable from the parking lot, whose loss would only slow work for a few hours.

              Questions. (a) Compute the four scores and their bands, and explain the ranking to the owner in the vocabulary of the lesson. (b) Rate and place the new access point. (c) Why does the technician write a reason next to every rating, and what is the register's role in the Integrative Project?

              Model answer. (a) FS01: 5 × 3 = 15 (high band, ≥ 15); e-mail: 4 × 5 = 20 (high); NAS01: 4 × 2 = 8 (medium, 8 to 14); printer: 1 × 3 = 3 (low, ≤ 7). The score combines two estimates of a risk — the impact if the asset is lost, disclosed or altered, and the exposure, which stands for the likelihood that a threat reaches it. The file server has the highest impact, but it cannot be reached from the Internet (exposure 3: reachable by all staff inside the office only), whereas the e-mail accounts are reachable by anyone on the Internet at any time (exposure 5). A high impact with a lower likelihood produces a smaller risk than a slightly lower impact with the highest likelihood; the register orders risks, not values. (b) Impact 2 (some tasks are slower for a few hours); exposure 4 (reachable from outside the office — radio signal). Score 2 × 4 = 8, medium band, the same as the Class 2 result for AP01. It is added to the register as a new asset with an identifier, because a first inventory is rarely complete and finding what is missing is part of Lab 1. (c) A score is a help for deciding, not a measurement; two people can give different ratings, so the reason for every rating is recorded (as comments in the program) so that the ranking can be checked and defended in front of the owner. The register is deliverable D1: Lab 1 starts from it to map the network and decide what must be monitored first; the same idea — priority, because money, time and staff are limited — returns in every topic.

              Case study 5

              One payroll file, three checks (Class 2, Lesson 1.2)

              Situation. On September 15 the owner of Grey Pine approves payroll_2026-09.csv; the technician restricts its permissions to the owner and the payroll group and records its SHA-256 hash. On September 17 the routine check shows that every user of the server can now read the file, that the hash differs, and that the file has a fourth row: an unknown payee, 9,999 dollars. The technician's first instinct is to delete the row, restore the permissions and tell nobody, "since it is fixed".

              Questions. (a) Which properties of the CIA (Confidentiality, Integrity, Availability) triad have been lost, and which check reveals each? (b) What does the different hash prove, and what does it not prove? (c) What must the technician do, and which rule of the course requires it?

              Model answer. (a) Confidentiality is lost: the permission check shows that persons who are not authorized (every user) can read the payroll data. Integrity is lost: the hash comparison shows that the content is no longer the approved content — a fourth row was added without approval. Availability is intact: the file can still be reached and used. (b) A different SHA-256 hash proves that at least one byte of the content changed after the baseline was recorded; the hash is deterministic, has a fixed length of 64 hexadecimal characters, and changes completely when a single character changes. It does not say who changed the file, when, exactly what was changed or whether the change was approved; those answers come from the event logs and from the people concerned. A hash is not encryption either: it hides nothing, and the file remains readable. (c) He records the evidence — both hashes, both permission values and the time of the check — informs the owner immediately, and keeps the file as it is for the analysis. Correcting silently would destroy the evidence and could hide a fraud. The Code of Ethics of the Legal Notice (section 9) requires reporting findings accurately and completely and never concealing an incident; the competency requires work under supervision and clear communication with stakeholders. The same discipline appears in Lesson 1.5 (preserve the evidence before changing anything) and in Lesson 1.4 (the technician recommends; the person responsible approves). In Lab 2 this baseline becomes an alert ("the hash of a protected file differs from its baseline", file integrity monitoring); in Lab 3 the same anomaly is diagnosed and reported.

              Case study 6

              A Friday morning on TE-FS01 (Class 3, Lessons 1.3 and 1.4)

              Situation. The logon records of the Trois-Érables file server on Friday, September 18, 2026 contain, among fifteen records: 09:03:40 4625 m.tremblay from 192.168.56.21, then 09:03:52 4624 m.tremblay from the same address; 09:10:01 to 09:10:11, six 4625 events on administrator from 203.0.113.45, two seconds apart; 09:14:20 to 09:16:20, five 4625 events from 198.51.100.77, one every thirty seconds, each on a different account; 09:31:05, a 4624 for j.roy from 198.51.100.77. The server locks an account after five consecutive failures; a detection rule alerts when one source produces five failures within ten minutes.

              Questions. (a) Classify the three patterns and name the property harmed. (b) At what times do the preventive control and the detective control react to each attack, and why does the lockout miss one of them? (c) How much time did detection give the office, and what may the technician do with it?

              Model answer. (a) m.tremblay: one failure then a success twelve seconds later, same account, same workstation inside the office — a typing mistake, not an attack. 203.0.113.45: six failures in ten seconds, always on one account, from one external address — no person types that fast; many passwords against one account is a brute-force attack. 198.51.100.77: one failure per account across five accounts, thirty seconds apart — one password tried against many accounts is password spraying, designed so that no account reaches the lockout limit; the success as j.roy fifteen minutes later means the attacker found a valid password. Password attacks harm confidentiality (a credential is disclosed). (b) Brute force: at 09:10:09 the fifth consecutive failure on administrator arrives — the account locks (event 4740 would record it) and the alert fires in the same second, because the source has produced five failures within ten minutes; both controls worked. Spraying: the lockout never reacts, because it counts consecutive failures per account and each account received only one; the detection rule counts failures per source, not per account, and fires at 09:16:20, two minutes after the first attempt. This is the data behind "prevention is never sufficient" and behind defense in depth: two independent controls react differently to the same log. (c) Between the alert at 09:16:20 and the attacker's logon at 09:31:05 there are 14 minutes 45 seconds. If someone reads the alert and obtains the approval to block the source during that time, no account is compromised; if nobody reads it, detection had no effect. The technician's part is to write the incident note — what was observed, when, on which system, from which source — and recommend actions (block the source on the firewall, disable and reset j.roy, review what the account opened); the technician does not block or disable on a production network without the approval of the person responsible (Legal Notice section 7.4). If the file server holds personal information of clients, the person responsible must decide about the register of confidentiality incidents and, if there is a risk of serious injury, the notification of the CAI (Commission d'accès à l'information du Québec).

              Case study 7

              "It is slow" twice on the same week-end (Class 4, Subject 1.5)

              Situation. At Atelier Nord-Ouest, Report A (Saturday 13:10): sending a quote to the plotter takes forty seconds instead of four, every Saturday afternoon; FS01 shows processor 60–75 % and disk writing 40–60 MB/s from 13:00 to 15:00 every Saturday for five weeks; no failed sign-ins above the usual two or three; no new accounts or services; the change record of August 15 moved the archive job to BK01 to Saturday 13:00. Report B (Sunday 09:20): two users are locked out, the server was slow during the night, and files with a strange extension appear in the shared folder; between 01:40 and 02:35, 412 failed sign-ins for three accounts from one address, one successful sign-in at 02:05, processor 96 %, disk writing 180 MB/s, 1,940 files with an extension absent from the baseline, one outbound connection to a never-seen address, and the Windows security log cleared at 02:31. A junior colleague wants to reboot FS01 "to clean it up".

              Questions. (a) Apply the four questions to each report and give the verdict. (b) Which of the five beginner mistakes is the colleague about to make, and what must be exported first? (c) What legal duty appears in Report B, and who decides it?

              Model answer. (a) Report A — Q1: one server, Saturday afternoons, five weeks. Q2: yes, a documented change (August 15) and a scheduled job explain it. Q3: no trace of an actor. Q4: inside the baseline recorded for Saturday afternoons. Verdict: Performance; the correction is a scheduling decision taken with the service owner, recorded as a service request with the measurements attached. Report B — Q1: the file server, Sunday night, fifty-five minutes. Q2: no job is scheduled at that time and nobody works on Sunday. Q3: yes — lockouts, a success after failures, mass file creation, a new destination, a cleared log. Q4: far outside the Sunday baseline. Verdict: Security incident that also produces a performance symptom, which makes it a Both case in the reporting: the security procedure runs first, and the processor and disk measurements are kept as evidence of impact. The pattern (failures then success, mass creation of files with a new extension, an outbound connection, a cleared log) matches ransomware preceded by a password attack. (b) "Rebooting or reimaging first": a restart destroys memory contents, running process lists and temporary files, and the timeline can no longer be rebuilt. Export first: the Windows security log, the file listing with times, and the firewall connection record. The cleared log at 02:31 is itself evidence — an action, and actions have authors. Do not delete the new files and do not run a cleaning tool. (c) Client files are involved, so the personal information rules apply: the incident is recorded in the register of confidentiality incidents and, where it presents a risk of serious injury, the CAI and the persons concerned are notified. That decision belongs to the person responsible for the protection of personal information, not to the technician; the technician's accurate and fast incident note is what makes a correct decision possible.

              Case study 8

              The clinic's inventory and the place for the sensor (Class 5, Lessons 2.1 and 2.2)

              Situation. The Fictiva clinic's documentation lists, among others: SW-CORE-01, a 24-port managed switch that powers the camera and the access point (forwards traffic; 9 dependent devices; no personal information; not Internet-facing); WS-XRAY-01, a workstation used by the hygienist that stores x-ray images (full operating system; a person uses it; personal information); CAM-DOOR-01, an entrance camera (firmware only; records people); a computer in the office that shares the patient database with eight colleagues and that nobody works on. The cable map lists WS-DENT-02 on switch port 8, but the inventory has no WS-DENT-02. Following the ten documented flows, SW-CORE-01 carries all ten, FW-EDGE-01 and MODEM-ISP-01 carry three each, AP-FRONT-01 two.

              Questions. (a) Classify the four devices and compute the priority points of the first three. (b) Where should the monitoring sensor be connected, how does it receive the traffic, and which devices are single points of failure? (c) What do you do about WS-DENT-02, and what must you never do?

              Model answer. (a) SW-CORE-01: forwards traffic → network equipment; 9 dependents (+4), no personal information, not Internet-facing, no interactive user → 4 points → High. WS-XRAY-01: does not forward traffic, has a full operating system, a person uses it → workstation; personal information (+2), interactive user (+1) → 3 points → Medium. CAM-DOOR-01: no full operating system → other endpoint; personal information (+2) → 2 points → Medium. The computer sharing the patient database offers a service and nobody works on it → server, whatever it looks like; the family is decided by what a device does. (b) The sensor goes on SW-CORE-01, which carries 10 of 10 flows (100 %): it is where the traffic converges. It receives a copy of the traffic through port mirroring (SPAN, Switched Port Analyzer), a feature of a managed switch that sends a copy of chosen ports to the sensor's port; the cable map tells you which port to mirror. SW-CORE-01, FW-EDGE-01, MODEM-ISP-01 and AP-FRONT-01 are single points of failure: the clinic is a tree topology (14 devices, 13 links, no loop), so every device in the middle of a path stops everything behind it. (c) Record the difference as a finding: either the inventory forgot a computer or the computer was removed and the cable map was never updated. Compare the documents with each other and, with the owner's authorization, with what the network itself reports (the switch's MAC address table, the DHCP lease list); ask the owner which version is correct; update the documents with a new version number and date. Never fill the gap by scanning the network without written authorization: a scan is an intrusive act that the target records as an attack (Legal Notice section 7.6), and Lab 1 involves no scanning.

              Case study 9

              "Can we do that here?" and "What must we watch?" (Class 6, Lessons 2.3 and 2.4)

              Situation. The register of Val-des-Pins says: CAD 1,500 approved, no new server (C-01); provider 6 hours per month, nobody on call (C-02); personal information under Law 25, retention 90 days (C-03); the CNC vendor contract voids the warranty if third-party software is installed on CNC-PC-01 (C-04); guest Wi-Fi traffic must never be captured (C-05); NAS-01 has 1.2 TB free (C-07); monitoring traffic ceiling 5 Mbit/s (C-08); CNC-PC-01 runs Windows 7 (C-09); SW-02 is unmanaged (C-10); clocks differ by 4 minutes (C-11). The technician proposes: full packet capture of the Internet link all day (a dedicated computer, CAD 900, about 30 Mbit/s); a monitoring agent on CNC-PC-01; capture of the guest Wi-Fi; and, as a monitoring need, "install an antivirus on the workstations".

              Questions. (a) Give the verdict on the three activities, with the constraint that decides each and the adaptation when one exists. (b) Why is "install an antivirus" not a monitoring need, and how is a need written? (c) What happens to the need "detect password guessing on CNC-PC-01", and why must it not be silently dropped?

              Model answer. (a) Full packet capture: refused as written — it breaks C-08 (30 Mbit/s against a 5 Mbit/s ceiling) and would exhaust the budget and the storage; feasible with adaptation: flow records, the connection summaries the firewall already produces (about 40 events per second of 120 bytes, no extra hardware). Agent on CNC-PC-01: breaks C-04 and C-09 (no software allowed on that device); feasible with adaptation: watch it from the network side with availability checks plus the FW-01 log. Capture of the guest Wi-Fi: not feasible now — C-05 is a hard legal and policy constraint (the guests did not consent), and no lighter version exists. Each verdict is recorded in the constraints section of the plan, with the constraint identifier. (b) A need is written before any tool is chosen; "install an antivirus" names a tool and says nothing about what must be detected. A need states one event to detect on one asset, with the observable (a number or pattern), the data source the constraints allow, the detection time objective, and who is told: "On WS-01..06 (criticality 2), detect a malware infection by observing an antivirus detection or outbound connections to unusual destinations in the antivirus console or the firewall log, within 15 minutes; notify the provider and the owner." The alert (Lesson 3.5) and the tool (Lesson 3.2) come afterwards. (c) Question 4 of the method ("where would we see it, among the sources the constraints allow?") has no answer: C-04 and C-09 remove the Windows event log from CNC-PC-01's usable sources, and password guessing is not visible in the firewall log or the availability check. The need is recorded as a gap, with the constraint that causes it, a compensating measure if one exists (the firewall sees every connection the device makes) or the owner's decision. A written gap can be prioritized, compensated or accepted; an unwritten gap is a surprise waiting to happen. The worked example finds 27 needs, 24 covered and 3 gaps, all three on CNC-PC-01; the gaps weigh in the prioritization of Lesson 2.5 and are the first items of the optimization proposed in Lab 3 (Lesson 6.3).

              Case study 10

              The order of work for Val-des-Pins (Class 7, Lesson 2.5)

              Situation. Ratings: FW-01 criticality 3, exposure 3; SRV-FILE-01 3 and 2; MAIL-CLOUD 3 and 2; PC-ACCT-01 3 and 2; NAS-01 3 and 1; PC-SHOP-01 1 and 3; PRN-01 1 and 2. Envelope: 2,275 MB and 60 minutes per day. Costs: FW-01 log 850 MB / 15 min; SRV-FILE-01 log 600 / 15; MAIL-CLOUD audit log 60 / 10; PC-ACCT-01 log 120 / 5; NAS-01 backup reports 5 / 5; PC-SHOP-01 log 60 / 5. The algorithm has already included FW-01, MAIL-CLOUD, PC-ACCT-01, SW-01 (150 / 5), SRV-FILE-01 and the reduced CNC-PC-01 activity (90 / 5), reaching 1,870 MB and 55 minutes, then AP-01's wireless log (80 / 5) brings the time to 60 minutes and NAS-01 is deferred.

              Questions. (a) Compute the scores and tiers of the seven assets, and explain why PC-SHOP-01 and NAS-01 have the same score with opposite profiles. (b) Among the four assets scored 6, why does MAIL-CLOUD come before SRV-FILE-01? (c) Is the deferral of NAS-01 acceptable? What does the technician do, and how is it recorded?

              Model answer. (a) FW-01 3 × 3 = 9 (Tier 1); SRV-FILE-01, MAIL-CLOUD and PC-ACCT-01 3 × 2 = 6 (Tier 1); NAS-01 3 × 1 = 3 (Tier 2); PC-SHOP-01 1 × 3 = 3 (Tier 2); PRN-01 1 × 2 = 2 (Tier 3). NAS-01 is critical but almost unreachable (reached only by the nightly backup job, one administrator account, current firmware, no incident); PC-SHOP-01 holds nothing of value but is wide open (browsing allowed, unsupported operating system, shared account, adware last year). Multiplication places both in the middle: an asset needs both a serious consequence and a real likelihood to deserve continuous attention; with addition the two would score 4 and a critical-and-exposed asset 6, and the distinction between "worth watching" and "watch first" would almost disappear. (b) The three tie-breaking rules apply in sequence: higher criticality first (equal, 3); higher exposure (equal, 2); then the lower daily cost — the cloud sign-in log costs 60 MB per day against 600 MB for the file server log, and a cheaper activity gives protection sooner for the same budget. FW-01 comes first of all with a score of 9. (c) No. NAS-01 is the recovery path of every Tier 1 asset: a backup that nobody checks leaves the whole plan without a way back after ransomware or a disk failure. A dependency is one of the two override reasons accepted without argument (the other is a legal obligation on an asset holding personal information). The technician overrides the computed order: the backup reports (5 MB / 5 min) are swapped in and the AP-01 wireless client log is deferred with a review date (October 16). The override is written in section 6 of the plan ("included by override — dependency: recovery path of every Tier 1 asset"), the deferred activity goes in section 7 with its reason, the decision maker and the review date, and the envelope ends at 1,875 of 2,275 MB (82 %) and 60 of 60 minutes (100 %). A gap that is written down is a decision; a gap that is not written down is a surprise.

              PART C

              45 multiple-choice questions (MCQ, one correct answer each)

              0 of 45 answered

              Each question has four options and exactly one correct answer. Read the hint only if you are stuck. The line Covers names the class, the lesson and the sub-section of the lecture module.

              MCQ 1 to 7

              Class 1 — Introduction to Preventative Monitoring

              0 / 7
              MCQ 1Covers: Class 1 · Lesson 1.1 (The course outline and the competency) · "Ponderation 2-3-1"

              In the ponderation 2-3-1 of 420-1C1-DW, what does the middle number mean?

              Hint: the three numbers are always read in the same order: theory, hands-on work, study.

              Answer: c) — The order is theory (2), laboratory or practical work (3), personal study (1). The 75 hours and the 2 2/3 credits are computed from these numbers; the number of quizzes comes from the evaluation plan.

              MCQ 2Covers: Class 1 · Lesson 1.1 · "The competency statement: EZ01"

              Which of the following is a performance criterion, in the sense used by the competency EZ01?

              Hint: a criterion is the wording used to judge quality; an element names the work; the context names the conditions.

              Answer: a) — Performance criteria are observable standards ("accurate interpretation of available data"). b) and d) are elements of the competency (sub-abilities); c) is part of the achievement context.

              MCQ 3Covers: Class 1 · Lesson 1.2 (The schedule and the evaluation plan) · "The two rules that decide whether you pass"

              A student has 88 % accumulated before the final examination and obtains 52 % on the final. What grade is recorded for the course?

              Hint: the final examination is the summative assessment element.

              Answer: d) — Rule 1: a final examination result below 60 % is a failure of the course, and the recorded grade for the whole course becomes that examination grade. The 73 % average is never computed.

              MCQ 4Covers: Class 1 · Lesson 1.3 (What preventative monitoring actually is) · "A distinction students are marked down for confusing"

              Which type of security control is monitoring?

              Hint: controls are classified by when they act.

              Answer: b) — Monitoring records that something happened; it cannot stop it. It is called preventative because it aims at an early stage of an attack, when detection still leaves time for someone to apply a preventive or corrective control. The monitoring does not prevent; it enables prevention.

              MCQ 5Covers: Class 1 · Lesson 1.3 · "The statistics of a baseline"

              The failed logons per hour on a server have a mean μ of 6 and a standard deviation σ of 2 over one representative week. With the μ + 3σ convention, which hourly count is the first to be flagged?

              Hint: compute the threshold, then look for the first value strictly above it.

              Answer: b) — μ + 3σ = 6 + 3 × 2 = 12. A value equal to 12 is on the line; 13 is the first value above it. About 99.7 % of normal observations fall within three standard deviations of the mean for an approximately normal distribution.

              MCQ 6Covers: Class 1 · Lesson 1.4 (Building the laboratory environment) · "The five network modes"

              Which virtual network adapter mode is prohibited in this course because it places the virtual machine directly on your home or campus network?

              Hint: which mode makes the guest look like another physical computer on your real network?

              Answer: d) — A bridged adapter exposes the guest fully to the real network; a capture inside the "laboratory" then records other people's traffic and can become interception under section 184 of the Criminal Code. NAT is used briefly for updates; host-only and internal are the permitted modes.

              MCQ 7Covers: Class 1 · Lesson 1.3 · "Where the observations come from"

              Which data source records who spoke to whom, on which port, for how long and with how many bytes, but without the payload?

              Hint: the source that is far smaller and far less privacy-invasive than a full capture.

              Answer: a) — Flow records contain no payload, so they are small and answer perhaps nine investigative questions in ten in a small network; full packet capture is reserved for the tenth.

              MCQ 8 to 15

              Class 2 — Foundations of Cybersecurity, part 1

              0 / 8
              MCQ 8Covers: Class 2 · Lesson 1.1 (What cybersecurity is and why organizations need it) · "A working definition"

              Which list gives the six unwanted actions that cybersecurity protects against, in the definition used by the course?

              Hint: the definition follows the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security and the NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology) glossary; d) is a list of attack types, not of actions.

              Answer: c) — The definition names six unwanted actions; the word "unauthorized" is its centre. The three CIA (Confidentiality, Integrity, Availability) properties group these six actions.

              MCQ 9Covers: Class 2 · Lesson 1.1 · "The vocabulary of risk"

              "One password shared by the whole staff for the accounting application" is an example of which term?

              Hint: it is a weakness that a threat can use.

              Answer: b) — A vulnerability is a weakness a threat can use. A threat is a possible cause of an unwanted event (a criminal group, a mistaken employee, a power failure); a control reduces a risk; an incident is a harmful event established by analysis.

              MCQ 10Covers: Class 2 · Lesson 1.1 · "Why organizations need it — 2. Incidents are frequent"

              According to the Statistics Canada survey on the impact of cybercrime on Canadian businesses in 2023, which cybersecurity activity did businesses report most often?

              Hint: it is the subject of this course, reported by 46 % of businesses.

              Answer: d) — Monitoring of network and business systems was the most common activity (46 %). Only 26 % had a written policy, 22 % had insurance and 13 % reported an incident to the police.

              MCQ 11Covers: Class 2 · Lesson 1.2 (The three security properties) · "How a change is detected: the hash"

              A file's SHA-256 (Secure Hash Algorithm, 256-bit) hash computed today differs from the hash recorded when the file was approved. What does this prove?

              Hint: be exact about what the comparison proves and what other sources must supply.

              Answer: a) — A different hash proves only that at least one byte changed. Who, when, what and whether the change was approved come from the event logs and from the people concerned. A hash is not encryption and hides nothing.

              MCQ 12Covers: Class 2 · Lesson 1.2 · "How availability is measured"

              An uptime of 99.9 % allows how much interruption per year?

              Hint: 8,760 hours in a year multiplied by the unavailable fraction.

              Answer: c) — 8,760 × 0.001 = 8.76 hours. 99 % allows 87.6 hours (about 3.65 days) and 99.99 % about 53 minutes.

              MCQ 13Covers: Class 2 · Lesson 1.2 · "Rating the impact: low, moderate or high"

              An asset is rated high for confidentiality, moderate for integrity and low for availability. Under the FIPS (Federal Information Processing Standards) 199 method used in the course, what is its overall impact level?

              Hint: one serious weakness is enough to cause serious harm.

              Answer: b) — The overall level is the highest of the three levels: one severe impact makes the asset high-impact whatever the other two answers are.

              MCQ 14Covers: Class 2 · Lesson 1.3 (The lab environment) · "How virtualization works"

              Why is a snapshot not a backup?

              Hint: think about what happens when the disk that holds the virtual machine fails.

              Answer: d) — A snapshot is a recorded state kept on the same disk as the machine; it protects against a broken exercise, not against a broken disk. A backup lives elsewhere.

              MCQ 15Covers: Class 2 · Lesson 1.3 · "The four environments of the program"

              Which statement about the AWS (Amazon Web Services) Academy Learner Lab is correct?

              Hint: remember the four facts about the Learner Lab and the shared responsibility model.

              Answer: a) — No credit card is requested; only some services and two regions are permitted; under the shared responsibility model the provider secures buildings, hardware and hypervisor, while the customer secures the operating system, accounts, network rules and data — monitoring is the customer's part.

              MCQ 16 to 23

              Class 3 — Common types of cyberattacks and basic cyber defense concepts

              0 / 8
              MCQ 16Covers: Class 3 · Lesson 1.3 (Common types of cyberattacks) · "Six terms to use with precision"

              Which of the following is not a cyberattack in the sense defined in Lesson 1.3?

              Hint: the word "deliberate" is in the definition.

              Answer: c) — A cyberattack is a deliberate action by a threat actor against confidentiality, integrity or availability. A disk failure harms availability but is an accident.

              MCQ 17Covers: Class 3 · Lesson 1.3 · "Attack type 4: password attacks"

              A source address produces one failed logon on each of twelve different accounts, one every thirty seconds, and no account is locked. Which attack is this?

              Hint: one or two passwords against many accounts, designed to stay under the lockout limit.

              Answer: d) — Password spraying reverses brute force: a few common passwords against many accounts, so no account reaches the number of failures that would lock it. Credential stuffing uses stolen pairs of account names and passwords from another website.

              MCQ 18Covers: Class 3 · Lesson 1.3 · "Table 3: Windows event identifiers"

              Which Windows Security log event identifier records that an account failed to log on?

              Hint: it is the event every password attack produces.

              Answer: b) — 4625 is a failed logon; 4624 a successful logon; 4740 an account locked out; 1102 the audit log cleared.

              MCQ 19Covers: Class 3 · Lesson 1.3 · "Attack type 6: on-path attack"

              On a local network, the same IP (Internet Protocol) address is seen associated with two different hardware (MAC (Media Access Control)) addresses. Which attack does this trace suggest?

              Hint: the attacker sends false address announcements so that other computers send their traffic to it.

              Answer: a) — In ARP spoofing the attacker's computer announces itself under another device's address; the switch address table then shows one address with two hardware addresses. Confidentiality and integrity are harmed.

              MCQ 20Covers: Class 3 · Lesson 1.4 (Basic cyber defense concepts) · "Detection needs three things"

              A rule that raises an alert when a count passes a limit within a period of time — for example five failed logons from one source in ten minutes — is which kind of rule?

              Hint: a signature matches the known pattern of a specific attack; this rule counts.

              Answer: c) — A threshold rule fires when a count passes a limit within a time window. A signature rule fires when the data matches the known pattern of a specific attack.

              MCQ 21Covers: Class 3 · Lesson 1.4 · "Response: five steps, under supervision"

              During the response to a confirmed incident, which action is not the monitoring technician's decision to take alone on a production network?

              Hint: a containment action changes the system and can interrupt legitimate users.

              Answer: d) — Disabling an account, blocking an address or shutting down a server are containment actions that need the approval of the person responsible for the system (Legal Notice section 7.4). The technician detects, analyzes, documents, reports and recommends.

              MCQ 22Covers: Class 3 · Lesson 1.4 · "Real-life example 2: which defense function reacted?"

              In the Class 3 example, the account lockout (five consecutive failures) never reacted to the password spraying. Why?

              Hint: the lockout counts consecutive failures per account; the detection rule counts failures per source.

              Answer: b) — Spraying gives each account one or two attempts, so no account reaches five consecutive failures. The detection rule counts by source and fired at 09:16:20; only detection saw that attack.

              MCQ 23Covers: Class 3 · Lesson 1.4 · "Figure 3: the three functions work as a cycle" (NIST CSF 2.0)

              In the NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology) Cybersecurity Framework 2.0, which two functions form the foundation described as "know the rules, and know the network"?

              Hint: Protect corresponds to prevention, Detect to detection, Respond and Recover to response; the two others come first.

              Answer: a) — The six functions are Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond and Recover. Govern and Identify are the foundation — Topic 2 and Lab 1 of this course.

              MCQ 24 to 29

              Class 4 — Security issues versus performance issues; close of Topic 1

              0 / 6
              MCQ 24Covers: Class 4 · Subject 1.5 (Security issues versus performance issues) · "1.5.1 Five words that must mean the same thing for everyone"

              Which statement is correct?

              Hint: a tool observes an event, a rule turns some events into an alert, a human decides whether it is an incident.

              Answer: d) — An event is neutral; an alert is a claim made by a tool, not a fact; an incident is a person's conclusion from evidence. A false negative is the absence of an alert when something abnormal did happen.

              MCQ 25Covers: Class 4 · Subject 1.5 · "1.5.3 What a security issue is — The point that decides most cases"

              What is the element that distinguishes a security issue from a performance issue?

              Hint: a performance issue is explained by demand, faults and change.

              Answer: c) — Neither severity nor slowness decides: a completely stopped service is often a failed disk, and a service that runs perfectly may be the one being read by an intruder. Traces of an actor decide the classification.

              MCQ 26Covers: Class 4 · Subject 1.5 · "1.5.5 The four-question triage — The decision rule"

              The evidence does not answer the question "Is there evidence of an actor?". Which verdict applies, and what follows?

              Hint: never close a case as "just slow" because no one found the cause.

              Answer: b) — When question 3 cannot be answered, the verdict is Undetermined: preserve the data, widen the collection, set a temporary alert and a review time, and inform the supervisor in writing.

              MCQ 27Covers: Class 4 · Subject 1.5 · "1.5.7 Five mistakes beginners make"

              Why must a technician not reboot a server before the classification of a report is decided?

              Hint: export first, act second.

              Answer: a) — If the verdict turns out to be security, the evidence is gone and the timeline cannot be rebuilt. The rule from Lesson 1.5.6: preserve the evidence before changing anything.

              MCQ 28Covers: Class 4 · Recap of Topic 1 · "1.4 Cyber defence concepts" (controls by nature)

              A monthly review of who holds which access rights is which kind of control, by nature?

              Hint: "by nature" groups controls as technical, administrative/managerial, operational or physical; d) is a classification by moment.

              Answer: c) — A policy or an access review is administrative or managerial; a firewall rule is technical; a log review carried out by people is operational; a lock on the server cabinet is physical.

              MCQ 29Covers: Class 4 · Recap of Topic 1 · "Turning Topic 1 into the monitoring priority list of Atelier Nord-Ouest"

              In the Class 4 priority list (impact 1–3 × exposure 1–3), the router RTR01 has impact 3 and exposure 3, and the backup server BK01 has impact 3 and exposure 1. Which tiers do they receive?

              Hint: Tier 1 is a score of 6 or more, Tier 2 is 3 to 5, Tier 3 is 2 or less.

              Answer: d) — RTR01: 3 × 3 = 9, Tier 1. BK01: 3 × 1 = 3, Tier 2. Tier 1 assets are the ones instrumented in Lab 2.

              MCQ 30 to 35

              Class 5 — Network components, documentation and topology

              0 / 6
              MCQ 30Covers: Class 5 · Lesson 2.1 (Network components) · "2.1.1 What a network is made of"

              Why does the monitoring plan start with the asset inventory?

              Hint: "you cannot monitor what you do not know".

              Answer: b) — This is why the first CIS (Center for Internet Security) Critical Security Control is Inventory and Control of Enterprise Assets, and why the NIST Cybersecurity Framework places asset management at the start of its Identify function.

              MCQ 31Covers: Class 5 · Lesson 2.1 · "2.1.4 Network equipment" (switch)

              How does a switch decide to which port it forwards a frame?

              Hint: switches work at layer 2 of the OSI (Open Systems Interconnection) model.

              Answer: a) — The switch learns which MAC address is reached through which port and forwards each frame only there; a frame for an unknown address goes to all ports. b) describes a router; c) a hub; d) a firewall.

              MCQ 32Covers: Class 5 · Lesson 2.2 (Reading network documentation and topology diagrams) · "2.2.3 Reading the addresses on a diagram"

              How many addresses can be given to devices in the subnet 192.168.10.0/24?

              Hint: .0 identifies the network and .255 is the broadcast address.

              Answer: d) — A /24 network has 256 addresses; the first identifies the network and the last is the broadcast address, leaving 254 usable addresses (.1 to .254). The same prefix is written as the mask 255.255.255.0.

              MCQ 33Covers: Class 5 · Lesson 2.2 · "2.2.2 Physical and logical diagrams"

              Which question is answered by the logical network diagram rather than the physical one?

              Hint: the logical diagram ignores rooms and racks.

              Answer: c) — The logical diagram shows networks, address ranges, VLAN (Virtual Local Area Network) numbers, gateways and firewall zones; the physical diagram shows rooms, racks, ports, jacks and cable types.

              MCQ 34Covers: Class 5 · Lesson 2.2 · "2.2.4 Topologies"

              The Fictiva clinic's network has 14 devices and 13 links and no loop. Which statement follows?

              Hint: N devices with N − 1 links and no loop is the definition of a tree.

              Answer: b) — The clinic is an extended star, a tree topology. For monitoring, the shape shows where traffic converges (the best observation point) and where one failure stops many devices.

              MCQ 35Covers: Class 5 · Lesson 2.2 · "2.2.6 When documentation and reality disagree"

              The cable map lists a workstation that the inventory does not contain. What does the technician do?

              Hint: a scan without written authorization is an intrusive act the target records as an attack.

              Answer: d) — Each difference is a finding to confirm with the owner; scanning without authorization is prohibited (Legal Notice section 7.6), and Lab 1 involves no scanning.

              MCQ 36 to 40

              Class 6 — Constraints and monitoring needs

              0 / 5
              MCQ 36Covers: Class 6 · Lesson 2.3 (Organizational and operational constraints) · "2.3.1 What a constraint is"

              "Detect a failed backup within 12 hours" is a…

              Hint: a constraint states what monitoring must respect; a requirement states what it must achieve.

              Answer: a) — Requirements are the subject of Lesson 2.4; constraints (money, people, law, contracts, capacity, legacy systems…) are the limits the plan must respect while meeting the requirements.

              MCQ 37Covers: Class 6 · Lesson 2.3 · "2.3.3 Operational constraints" (storage capacity)

              A firewall produces 25 events per second of 300 bytes each, kept for 90 days. Approximately how much storage is needed?

              Hint: bytes per event × events per second × 86,400 seconds per day × retention days.

              Answer: c) — 300 × 25 × 86,400 × 90 = 58,320,000,000 bytes, about 58 GB. This is the storage formula of the constraint register.

              MCQ 38Covers: Class 6 · Lesson 2.3 · "2.3.6 Worked example: the constraint register of Val-des-Pins"

              The CNC (Computer Numerical Control) vendor contract voids the warranty if third-party software is installed on CNC-PC-01. How is this constraint classified and adapted?

              Hint: a signed contract cannot be changed by the monitoring project.

              Answer: b) — C-04 is an organizational (contract) constraint, hard, impact 3 (blocks an activity). The plan watches the device from the network side; the same device also carries C-09 (Windows 7, unsupported).

              MCQ 39Covers: Class 6 · Lesson 2.4 (Identifying monitoring needs) · "2.4.1 What a monitoring need is"

              Why is "install an antivirus on the workstations" not a correctly written monitoring need?

              Hint: need, alert and tool are three different things, and the need is written before any tool is chosen.

              Answer: d) — A need is a precise statement: asset, event, observable with a number or pattern, data source allowed by the constraints, detection time objective, recipient. The tool comes in Topic 3.

              MCQ 40Covers: Class 6 · Lesson 2.4 · "2.4.5 Coverage and gaps"

              In the Val-des-Pins worked example, the program derives 27 needs, of which 24 are covered. On which asset are the three gaps, and why?

              Hint: password guessing, privilege change and disk almost full cannot be seen from the network side.

              Answer: a) — Without an agent or event log on CNC-PC-01, question 4 of the method has no answer for those three events; each gap is recorded with its constraint identifier and a compensating measure where one exists.

              Class 7 — Prioritizing monitoring activities

              MCQ 41Covers: Class 7 · Lesson 2.5.1 (Why prioritize) · "Real-life example 2.5.1 — The wish list does not fit"

              The owner approved 200 GB of disk for the monitoring virtual machine with a retention target of 90 days, and 5 hours per week of the technician's time. What is the daily resource envelope?

              Hint: 200 × 1024 ÷ 90; 5 hours ÷ 5 working days.

              Answer: c) — 200 GB × 1024 MB ÷ 90 days ≈ 2,275 MB per day; 5 hours ÷ 5 working days = 60 minutes per day. The wish list of ten activities costs 9,165 MB and 110 minutes.

              MCQ 42Covers: Class 7 · Lesson 2.5.2 (Criticality) · "High-water mark rule" and the NAS-01 example

              NAS-01 is rated confidentiality 3, integrity 3, availability 2. What is its criticality, and why is availability only 2?

              Hint: criticality is the highest of the three numbers; price is never rated.

              Answer: b) — One severe impact is enough to make an asset critical. The rule "rate the impact on the organization, never the replacement price" also applies.

              MCQ 43Covers: Class 7 · Lesson 2.5.3 (Exposure) · "Five exposure factors"

              PC-SHOP-01 allows web browsing, runs an unsupported operating system, is used through a shared "shop" account, holds no administrator rights to other assets, and had adware removed last year. What is its exposure?

              Hint: E1 Internet contact, E2 known weakness, E3 people and media, E4 privilege, E5 history; 4 or 5 is High.

              Answer: d) — E1 = 1, E2 = 1, E3 = 1, E4 = 0, E5 = 1: score 4, rating High (3) — on a machine whose criticality is 1. Exposure is independent of criticality.

              MCQ 44Covers: Class 7 · Lesson 2.5.4 (From two ratings to an order) · "Priority score"

              Why is the priority score computed by multiplying criticality by exposure rather than adding them?

              Hint: compare 3 × 1, 1 × 3 and 3 × 3 with 3 + 1, 1 + 3 and 3 + 3.

              Answer: a) — With multiplication the scores are 3, 3 and 9; with addition 4, 4 and 6, and the difference between "worth watching" and "watch first" almost disappears.

              MCQ 45Covers: Class 7 · Lesson 2.5.4 · "Override" and Real-life example 2.5.4

              Which two reasons for overriding the computed priority order are accepted without argument?

              Hint: NAS-01 was included by override because a backup that nobody checks leaves every Tier 1 asset without a recovery path.

              Answer: c) — Any other override must be explained in the plan and signed off by the owner. Ties are settled by the three tie-breaking rules, not by overrides.

              20 short-essay questions
