              Answer each in five to ten lines. The model answers list the points a complete answer contains; the grader looks for the reasoning and the exact vocabulary of the course, not for the wording.

              Essay 1 to 3

              Class 1 — Introduction to Preventative Monitoring

              0 / 3
              Essay 1Covers: Class 1 · Lesson 1.3 (What preventative monitoring actually is) · "The definition, one clause at a time" and "A distinction students are marked down for confusing"

              Give the definition of preventative monitoring and explain why it is a detective control although its name says "preventative".

              Hint: take the definition one clause at a time; then use the classification of controls by the moment at which they act.

              Model answer. Preventative monitoring is the continuous and systematic observation of a computer network and its systems, carried out in order to detect and report deviations from a known normal state early enough for action to be taken before damage occurs. Continuous: observation runs at all times; systematic: what is observed, how often and what counts as notable are decided in advance and written down; known normal state: the baseline, without which "unusual" has no meaning; detect and report: detection without reporting changes nothing; before damage occurs: the observation buys time. Controls are classified by when they act: preventive controls stop an event, detective controls record that it happened, corrective controls restore the state. Monitoring records; it cannot stop anything. It is called preventative because it aims at an early stage of an attack, where detection still leaves time for someone else to apply a preventive or corrective control. The monitoring does not prevent; it enables prevention.

              Why this is the expected answer. This is the exact wording and the exact distinction the lecture marks students down for confusing; the reports written in Labs 2 and 3 must state it this way.

              Essay 2Covers: Class 1 · Lesson 1.3 · "The statistics of a baseline" and "How detection quality is measured"

              Explain what a baseline is, how the threshold μ + 3σ is derived, and why raising or lowering the number three trades one detection error for another.

              Hint: mean, standard deviation, the 99.7 % property, false positives, false negatives, alert fatigue.

              Model answer. A baseline is a statistical description of normal behaviour, not a screenshot of a normal day: over a representative period (daily and weekly cycles included) you record many observations and compute the arithmetic mean μ (the centre of normal behaviour) and the standard deviation σ (how much normal behaviour varies). For an approximately normal distribution about 99.7 % of normal observations fall within three standard deviations of the mean, so a value above μ + 3σ is unusual enough to deserve a human's attention while rare enough not to flood the queue. Three is a working convention: raising it produces false negatives (real events with no alert — the failure that lets an incident proceed undetected); lowering it produces false positives (alerts with nothing behind them), which cost analyst time and cause alert fatigue, after which genuine alerts are dismissed by habit, so high false-positive rates produce false negatives indirectly. The baseline must be rebuilt when the network legitimately changes, because a stale baseline gives confident, wrong answers (criterion 5.1). Topic 6 is largely about choosing that number well.

              Why this is the expected answer. The question tests that the student can connect the statistics to the two error types and to the practical consequence, which is what tuning in Topic 6 will require.

              Essay 3Covers: Class 1 · Lesson 1.4 (Building the laboratory environment) · "Why the laboratory is isolated" and "Verify every download before you run it"

              State the three conditions of an Authorized Lab Environment and describe two checks you perform before a lab session that give evidence, rather than an assertion, that they hold.

              Hint: ownership or permission, segregation, fictional data; the pre-flight script and the checksum.

              Model answer. The three conditions must hold at once: (1) you own the environment or are expressly permitted to use it for the exercise; (2) it is disconnected from, or securely segregated from, any production, institutional, corporate, public or third-party network; (3) it contains no real personal data and no system belonging to anyone who has not consented in writing. Evidence, not assertion: the pre-flight conformity check asks the hypervisor for each machine's adapter modes (any bridged adapter fails the whole report, because it puts the guest on the real network and can turn a capture into interception under section 184), confirms that a snapshot exists for every machine (section 6.4), checks free disk space, checks that no real personal data is on the lab volume, and produces a dated report (deliverable D4) attached to every lab. Before installing any image, the SHA-256 checksum computed locally (Get-FileHash in PowerShell, sha256sum on Linux) is compared with the value the publisher published; unfamiliar links and files are checked with VirusTotal and Google Safe Browsing (Annex C). Professionals evidence isolation; they do not assert it.

              Why this is the expected answer. The lecture insists that a check must give a specific, actionable failure; the student must show both the conditions and the mechanics of verifying them.

              Essay 4 to 6

              Class 2 — Foundations of Cybersecurity, part 1

              0 / 3
              Essay 4Covers: Class 2 · Lesson 1.1 (What cybersecurity is) · "Why organizations need it" and "Who is responsible, and your role"

              Give three reasons why an office of nine people needs cybersecurity, each supported by a Canadian figure or a legal duty, and describe the role of the monitoring technician among the people responsible.

              Hint: Statistics Canada 2023; Law 25; the National Cyber Threat Assessment; owner, administrator, employee, technician.

              Model answer. (1) The work depends on digital systems: impacted Canadian businesses lost working time in four cases in ten, 36 hours on average (2021 data); an office that bills by the hour loses revenue directly. (2) Incidents are frequent and costly: in 2023 one business in six was impacted, recovery spending reached about 1.2 billion dollars (double 2021), scams and fraud hit half of impacted businesses, and the survey does not even count enterprises under 10 employees, which are found by the same automated searches as large ones — the National Cyber Threat Assessment 2025-2026 names ransomware the top cybercrime threat. (3) The office holds information that belongs to other people: under the Act respecting the protection of personal information in the private sector as amended by Law 25, the enterprise is responsible for the personal information it holds, must record every confidentiality incident in a register, must notify the CAI and the persons concerned when there is a risk of serious injury, and faces penalties up to 10 million dollars or 2 % of turnover (administrative) and 25 million or 4 % (penal). Also: clients, insurers and partners ask for proof. Roles: the owner decides the acceptable risk and pays for the controls (and is by default the person in charge of personal information); the administrator installs and maintains; every employee applies the rules; the monitoring technician watches the tools, sorts the alerts, analyzes what is abnormal and reports it clearly to the people who decide — under supervision, judged on ethics, priorities, communication and the confidentiality of the data collected.

              Why this is the expected answer. The outline's first learning outcome and criterion 1.1 require the student to justify security in organizational terms, with the figures the lecture supplied.

              Essay 5Covers: Class 2 · Lesson 1.2 (The three security properties) · "Working with the three properties together"

              Using two examples, show that one incident can touch several properties, and explain why the properties compete with one another and what follows for the choice of controls.

              Hint: the stolen laptop; ransomware that copies before encrypting; extra proofs of identity versus availability; the shared password.

              Model answer. A laptop without disk encryption stolen from a car loses confidentiality (the thief can read the files) and availability (the employee no longer has her computer). Ransomware that first copies the client files to the criminals' server and then encrypts them loses all three: confidentiality (copied), integrity (altered by the encryption), availability (unusable). A bookkeeper sending a tax return to the wrong client loses confidentiality only; a fourth payee added to the payroll file loses integrity only; a full disk loses availability with no attacker involved. The properties compete: every extra proof of identity protects confidentiality and slows or sometimes blocks a legitimate user, reducing availability; a password shared by the whole staff makes the application quickly available to everybody and destroys confidentiality and the ability to know who did what. There is no universal setting; each organization decides, asset by asset, which property matters most — the client project folder needs confidentiality and integrity, the plotter queue on a delivery day needs availability — and the choice is written down so that it can be defended. In an incident report, the first line names the property at risk, because it decides whom to inform and how urgent the matter is.

              Why this is the expected answer. Criterion 1.1 is "correct identification of issues linked to confidentiality, integrity and availability"; the examiner expects the student to reason per property, not to recite the acronym.

              Essay 6Covers: Class 2 · Lesson 1.3 (The lab environment) · "The network modes of a virtual machine" and "The rules of a safe lab"

              Compare the four network modes of a virtual machine and state the rule of the course. Explain why promiscuous mode is safe on a host-only network and dangerous on a bridged adapter.

              Hint: NAT, bridged, host-only, internal; who can reach whom; section 184; the most likely mistake in the course.

              Model answer. NAT (Network Address Translation): the guest reaches the Internet through the host's address; nobody from outside reaches it; two VirtualBox guests in NAT mode do not see each other; used only briefly, for updates and packages. Bridged: the guest reaches, and is reachable by, every device of the physical network (home, College, workplace); not used, because lab traffic would mix with other people's traffic. Host-only: the guest reaches the host and the other guests of the same host-only network, no Internet; the standard mode for lab traffic (VirtualBox default range 192.168.56.0/24). Internal network (VMware: LAN segment): only the guests attached to the same internal network, not even the host; for the strictest isolation. The rule: lab traffic travels on a host-only or internal network; a NAT adapter is connected only for the time of an update, then disconnected; bridged mode is not used unless a lab guide asks for it and explains how to do it safely (section 6.4). In promiscuous mode a network card accepts every frame that reaches it, not only the frames addressed to it; capture tools switch it on. On a host-only network the card sees only lab traffic; on a bridged adapter on a shared network the same capture records the communications of other people, which may constitute interception under section 184 of the Criminal Code (section 7.2). The most likely mistake in the course is capturing on the home or campus Wi-Fi "to have real traffic to analyze".

              Why this is the expected answer. The network mode is the single most important security setting of the laboratory, and the exam tests that the student can explain, not just name, the modes.

              Essay 7 to 9

              Class 3 — Common types of cyberattacks and basic cyber defense concepts

              0 / 3
              Essay 7Covers: Class 3 · Lesson 1.3 (Common types of cyberattacks) · "Attack type 4: password attacks" and "Real-life example 1"

              Explain how a monitoring technician distinguishes a typing mistake, a brute-force attack and password spraying in a logon log, and why password spraying defeats an account lockout policy.

              Hint: two counters per source address — failures and distinct accounts; events 4625 and 4624; five consecutive failures per account.

              Model answer. The technician reads four fields per record (time, event identifier, account, source) and keeps two counters per source address: the number of failures and the number of different accounts. A typing mistake is one failure (4625) followed by a success (4624) a few seconds later, same account, same workstation inside the office. Brute force is many failures on one account from one source at a speed no person types (six in ten seconds); it aims at one account with many passwords, so the lockout policy (five consecutive failures) reacts and event 4740 records it. Password spraying is the reverse: one or two common passwords against many accounts, one failure per account, spaced out; each account stays below the lockout limit, so the preventive control never reacts — only a detection rule that counts per source (five failures from one source within ten minutes) sees it. A success from the same source after the spread of failures means the attacker found a valid password and is the probable compromise to escalate. Credential stuffing is the variant that uses pairs stolen from another website. The conclusion is written as one result line per source (failures, distinct accounts, conclusion) and, in Lab 1, as two suspicious behaviours to watch on the file server.

              Why this is the expected answer. Criterion 1.2 requires precise differentiation between attack types; the two counters are the method the course teaches for exactly this case.

              Essay 8Covers: Class 3 · Lesson 1.4 (Basic cyber defense concepts) · "Prevention", "Detection needs three things", "Response"

              "Detection exists because prevention fails." Explain this sentence with the three functions of cyber defense, and name the three things detection needs in order to work.

              Hint: preventive, detective, corrective controls; zero-day, human error, insider, limited resources; data sources, baseline, rules.

              Model answer. Cyber defense is organized in three moments: prevention acts before the attack succeeds (patches, MFA (Multi-Factor Authentication), account lockout, firewall, least privilege, offline backups, awareness training); detection acts during or shortly after the attack and makes it visible (logging, monitoring tools, IDS (Intrusion Detection System), SIEM (Security Information and Event Management), file integrity checking, alerting on a baseline deviation); response acts after the incident is confirmed (preparation, analysis, containment, eradication and recovery, lessons learned). Prevention is necessary and never sufficient, for four reasons: a zero-day attack has no update; people make errors; an insider already holds authorized access; money and staff are limited, so some systems are always less protected. A professional defender therefore assumes some attacks pass and prepares to see them and act — an organization that monitors nothing learns about its incidents from a client, a bank or a journalist. Detection needs three things: data sources (event logs of servers and workstations, firewall and network equipment logs, captured traffic, security software alerts); a baseline (a recorded description of normal activity — without it nobody can say an activity is abnormal); detection rules — threshold rules (a count passing a limit within a time window) and signature rules (a match with the known pattern of an attack) — plus a person who reads the alert, since detection that nobody acts on has no effect. The three functions work as a cycle: lessons learned in the response improve prevention and detection.

              Why this is the expected answer. Criterion 1.3, appropriate illustration of cyber defense concepts; the recap names this sentence as the one to remember for the examination.

              Essay 9Covers: Class 3 · Lesson 1.4 · "Your part in the response: under supervision" and "In Québec: Law 25"

              Describe what a monitoring technician does and does not do when an alert turns out to be a real incident on a production network, and explain the legal step that a confidentiality incident adds in Québec.

              Hint: incident note; containment needs approval (section 7.4); register; CAI; person responsible for personal information.

              Model answer. The technician verifies the alert, determines what happened and which systems are affected, preserves the evidence, documents and reports: the most valuable product is a clear incident note — what was observed, when, on which system, from which source, and what is recommended (block the source on the firewall, disable and reset the compromised account, review what it opened). The technician does not decide alone to block an address, disable an account or shut down a server on a production network: a containment action changes the system and can interrupt legitimate users, so it needs the approval of the person responsible for that system (Legal Notice section 7.4 gives the same rule for laboratory work; measures that reach out to another system are prohibited in every course). In Québec, an incident involving personal information is a confidentiality incident under the Act as amended by Law 25: the organization must record it in its register and, if the incident presents a risk of serious injury, notify the Commission d'accès à l'information du Québec and the persons concerned. That decision belongs to the person responsible for the protection of personal information (by default the person with the highest authority), not to the technician — but this person can decide correctly only if the technician's note is accurate and arrives quickly. Speed of response is measured by the MTTR (Mean Time to Respond).

              Why this is the expected answer. The competency's achievement context ("under supervision") and its criteria (ethics, communication with stakeholders, confidentiality) are examined here in practical form.

              Essay 10 to 12

              Class 4 — Security issues versus performance issues; close of Topic 1

              0 / 3
              Essay 10Covers: Class 4 · Subject 1.5 (Security issues versus performance issues) · "1.5.2", "1.5.3" and "1.5.4"

              Define a performance issue and a security issue in words that do not overlap, and explain why the two look alike on the first screen of a monitoring tool.

              Hint: demand, faults, change versus an actor; users report symptoms, not causes; the two examinable facts.

              Model answer. A performance issue is a condition in which a system still behaves exactly as designed but delivers its function too slowly, with less capacity than required or with interruptions, because of demand, resource limits, faults or configuration; no unauthorized person is involved, and the evidence is quantitative and repeatable (it follows the load, a schedule, or a documented change). A security issue is a condition caused by, or indicating, an action that was not authorized, an attempt at such an action, or a weakness that makes it possible; its distinguishing element is the presence of an actor — a person, script or program acting outside its authorization — whose traces a machine fault never leaves (failures then a success at night, unexplained accounts or services, mass file creation, unknown destinations, cleared logs, mismatched hashes). They look alike because users report symptoms (slow, stopped, full, strange), and each symptom has a routine and a hostile explanation: a disk filling quickly may be a backup keeping more copies or ransomware writing encrypted copies; a saturated link may be updates or exfiltration; a workstation at full load may be an antivirus scan or mining software. Two facts are examinable: a security incident can produce a performance symptom (encryption, DoS (Denial of Service) and mining consume resources — the slowness is real but is not the cause), and a security incident can produce no performance symptom at all (copying a folder to a personal cloud, a hidden administrator account), which is why monitoring cannot be limited to performance counters.

              Why this is the expected answer. Criterion 1.4, clear distinction between performance and security issues, is examined by definition and by the reason the distinction is hard.

              Essay 11Covers: Class 4 · Subject 1.5 · "1.5.5 The four-question triage" and "The decision rule"

              Present the four-question triage, the four possible verdicts, and explain why the decision rule is deliberately asymmetric.

              Hint: scope and time; demand and change; actor; baseline; Security / Performance / Both / Undetermined; the cost of the two mistakes.

              Model answer. The four questions are asked in the same sequence, each answered with data you can point at: (1) What exactly is affected, and since when? — the report, the inventory, the monitoring history and the log times establish scope and start time. (2) Does demand or a change explain it? — active users and sessions, scheduled jobs, backup windows, update history and the change record show whether the measurement follows normal work. (3) Is there evidence of an actor? — authentication logs, account and group changes, new services and tasks, process lists, outbound connections, file creation patterns and integrity checks; this question decides most cases. (4) What does the baseline say? — the reference database for this asset, this hour, this day; without it questions 2 and 3 are guesses. Verdicts: traces of an actor with no authorization → Security (treated as an incident until disproved); no actor, and demand, a fault or a documented change explains values inside the baseline → Performance; actor traces and a resource exhausted → Both (security path first; the resource problem is a consequence); no answer to question 3 → Undetermined (preserve, raise the priority, escalate; never close a case as "just slow"). The rule is asymmetric because the two mistakes cost differently: calling a security incident a performance problem leaves an actor inside the network with time to continue; calling a performance problem a security incident costs an escalation and some wasted hours — the second mistake is corrected in a morning, the first one is corrected by a lawyer.

              Why this is the expected answer. The triage sheet is Appendix A of the Lab 1 plan and the reporting form of Lab 3; the exam expects the method, its evidence and its logic.

              Essay 12Covers: Class 4 · Recap of Topic 1 · "Turning Topic 1 into the monitoring priority list of Atelier Nord-Ouest"

              Explain how the Class 4 priority list uses all five subjects of Topic 1 at once, and state the scoring rule and the tiers.

              Hint: business reason, property, attack, control, kind of issue; impact 1–3 × exposure 1–3; Tier 1 ≥ 6, Tier 2 3–5, Tier 3 ≤ 2.

              Model answer. For each of the eight assets the list records: the business reason it matters (1.1); the property of the CIA (Confidentiality, Integrity, Availability) triad that matters most (1.2) — availability then integrity for the router, confidentiality and integrity for the file server, confidentiality for the access point; the most likely attack (1.3) — denial of service or exploitation of an exposed service on RTR01, ransomware or insider misuse on FS01, unauthorized association or interception on AP01, phishing leading to malware on the workstations; the defence concept that protects it (1.4); and the kind of issue you expect to see there (1.5). Then a priority: impact 3 if work stops or client information is exposed, 2 if work is slowed, 1 if minor; exposure 3 if reachable from the Internet or an untrusted network, 2 if every internal user reaches it daily, 1 if access is restricted; score = impact × exposure; Tier 1 is 6 or more (RTR01 9, FS01 6, AP01 6), Tier 2 is 3 to 5 (workstations 4, BK01 3), Tier 3 is 2 or less (plotter, printer, switch). The inventory file carries the words High, Medium and Low, converted to 3, 2 and 1 by the script, and the rule is written down so that the ranking can be defended in front of the owner — what criterion 2.3 asks in Topic 2. Tier 1 assets are instrumented in Lab 2 and analyzed in Lab 3.

              Why this is the expected answer. The recap is "performed instead of recited"; the exam may give a small inventory and ask for the same reasoning.

              Essay 13 to 14

              Class 5 — Network components, documentation and topology

              0 / 2
              Essay 13Covers: Class 5 · Lesson 2.1 (Network components) · "2.1.1 What a network is made of" and "Example 2.1"

              Explain why the asset inventory comes before any monitoring tool, describe the four device families and how a device is classified, and give the "what to monitor" column for each family.

              Hint: a tool watches only what it has been told about; CIS Control 1; role, not appearance; the four classification rules.

              Model answer. A monitoring tool watches only the devices it has been told about: a device missing from the inventory is not monitored, and if it fails or is attacked no alert is produced. This is why the first CIS (Center for Internet Security) Critical Security Control is Inventory and Control of Enterprise Assets, why the NIST Cybersecurity Framework starts its Identify function with asset management, and why the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security baseline controls ask organizations to identify systems and information before choosing protections. The inventory records at least hostname, address, role, location, owner and dependent devices. Four families, decided by what a device does: servers provide services to other devices and nobody works on them directly; workstations are endpoints used directly by one person with a full operating system; network equipment forwards traffic belonging to other devices; other endpoints are fixed-function devices running firmware only (printers, cameras, IoT (Internet of Things) devices). Classification rules in order: forwards traffic → network equipment; no full operating system → other endpoint; offers at least one service and no interactive user → server; a person uses it → workstation; otherwise the documentation is incomplete. What to monitor: network equipment — up/down status, port errors, traffic volume, device logs; servers — service availability, processor/memory/disk use, logons, backups; workstations — security event logs, failed logons, protection alerts, update level; other endpoints — reachability, firmware version, unexpected connections. Devices holding personal information (a camera, an x-ray workstation) receive extra priority because of Law 25.

              Why this is the expected answer. Element 2 of the competency starts with the inventory; Lab 1 grades it, and Lab 3 uses it to recognize a device that should not be on the network.

              Essay 14Covers: Class 5 · Lesson 2.2 (Reading network documentation) · "2.2.4 Topologies", "2.2.5 A method", "2.2.6 When documentation and reality disagree"

              Explain what a topology tells the monitoring plan, give the eight-step method to read a diagram, and state what a technician does and never does when documentation and reality disagree.

              Hint: where traffic converges; single points of failure; title block and legend first; findings confirmed with the owner; no scanning without written authorization.

              Model answer. The topology is the arrangement of nodes and links (physical: the cabling; logical: how data travels). For monitoring it tells two things: where traffic converges, which is the best place to observe it (SW-CORE-01 carries all ten flows of the clinic and receives the sensor through a mirror port), and where one failure stops many devices — in a tree topology (N devices, N − 1 links, no loop) every device in the middle of a path is a single point of failure for that path. The eight steps: is the document current (title block: name, version, date, owner); what do the symbols and lines mean (legend); where does the network end and what are its zones (boundaries); which devices exist and in which family (compare with the inventory); which networks and addresses (subnets, gateways, VLANs (Virtual Local Area Networks)); how does each important flow travel (follow the lines); where do flows converge and what has no backup; what is missing or contradictory. When documents and reality disagree, the technician compares the documents with each other, compares them — with the owner's authorization — with what the network reports (the switch's MAC (Media Access Control) address table, the DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol) lease list), records each difference as a finding, asks the owner which version is correct, and updates the documents with a new version number and date. The technician never fills a gap by scanning without written authorization: a scan is an intrusive act the target records as an attack (section 7.6); Lab 1 involves no scanning. Documentation is also sensitive: a complete diagram tells an attacker where to go (sections 7.5 and 7.9).

              Why this is the expected answer. Criterion 2.1 to 2.3 rest on reading documentation correctly; the exam tests the method and the rule.

              Essay 15 to 17

              Class 6 — Constraints and monitoring needs

              0 / 3
              Essay 15Covers: Class 6 · Lesson 2.3 (Organizational and operational constraints) · "2.3.1", "2.3.4" and "2.3.5"

              Define a constraint, distinguish organizational from operational and hard from soft, explain why constraints are examined before any tool is chosen, and describe the constraint register.

              Hint: a fact, not an opinion; four sources; eight columns; impact 1 to 3.

              Model answer. A constraint is a condition, imposed by the organization or by the way its network operates, that limits what monitoring can be done, how, when, where, by whom and at what cost; it is a fact traceable to a document, a contract, a law, a measurement or a decision of the owner — not an opinion. Organizational constraints come from the organization as a business (budget, people and skills, policies, laws, contracts, schedule, authorization, confidentiality of monitoring data); operational constraints come from the technical way the network runs (link and storage capacity, host processing capacity, availability requirements, legacy systems, equipment features such as SPAN (Switched Port Analyzer), SNMP (Simple Network Management Protocol) and syslog, segmentation, encryption and cloud, time synchronization, physical environment). A hard constraint cannot be changed by the project (a law, a signed contract, a safety rule); a soft one could be removed later with money, time or a decision, and only soft ones become recommendations in Lesson 6.5. Constraints come first because monitoring consumes resources, collects data about people, changes production systems, and is an offence without authorization whatever the intention (section 6.1) — a plan that ignores them is refused by the owner, breaks the network or breaks the law. Examination is thorough when it uses all four sources: documentation, interviews, observation, measurement. The register has fixed columns: ID (C-01…), family, category, description as a fact with its number or document, source, type (hard or soft), impact on monitoring (1 minor, 2 limits a choice, 3 blocks an activity), adaptation. It is the first deliverable of Lab 1 and one of the two inputs of prioritization.

              Why this is the expected answer. Criterion 2.1 is "thorough examination of the organizational and operational constraints"; the register is how thoroughness is shown.

              Essay 16Covers: Class 6 · Lesson 2.4 (Identifying monitoring needs) · "2.4.1", "2.4.3" and "2.4.5"

              Define a monitoring need, present the six-question method with the example of password guessing on SRV-FILE-01, and explain what happens when a need has no usable data source.

              Hint: asset and criticality; event; observable with a number; data source allowed by the constraints; detection time objective; recipient and first action; gap.

              Model answer. A monitoring need is a precise statement of one thing that must be observed on one asset, for one security or operational reason, together with the sign that would reveal it, the place where that sign is recorded, and the time within which it must be noticed; it is written before any tool is chosen — need, alert and tool are three different things. Six questions per asset: (1) what is the asset and how much does it need C, I and A — SRV-FILE-01: 3, 3, 3; (2) what could go wrong — someone guesses passwords against the logon, harming C and I; (3) what would we see, with a number — 10 or more failed logons from one source within 5 minutes (event 4625); (4) where would we see it, among the sources the constraints allow — the Windows Security event log, collected by activity A1; (5) how fast must we know — 15 minutes, long enough to ignore one mistyped password, short enough to act before the attacker succeeds; (6) who is told and what happens next — the provider's technician and the owner by e-mail; block the source on FW-01 and check the account. Written as one sentence, the row reads "N-01 — On SRV-FILE-01 (criticality 3), detect password guessing against the logon by observing 10 or more failed logons from one source within 5 minutes in the Windows Security event log, within 15 minutes; notify the provider and the owner." When question 4 has no answer (on CNC-PC-01 the no-software constraint removes the event log), the need is recorded as a gap, never silently dropped, with the constraint that causes it, a compensating measure if one exists (the firewall sees every connection the device makes) or the owner's decision. Coverage is the share of needs with at least one usable source; the coverage matrix shows the counts per asset and source; the example gives 27 needs, 24 covered, 3 gaps, all on CNC-PC-01.

              Why this is the expected answer. Criterion 2.2, identification of surveillance needs; the register is section 4 of the Lab 1 plan and every covered need becomes an alert rule in Lab 2.

              Essay 17Covers: Class 6 · Lesson 2.3 · "Employee monitoring in Québec" and Class 7 · "Legal reminder — facts about people"

              Explain the legal duties of an organization that monitors its own network in Québec, and the stricter rule that applies to you in this course.

              Hint: inform, limit, protect, retain no longer than needed; the CAI; systems and events, never people; sections 6.3, 6.7 and 7.2.

              Model answer. Monitoring a network necessarily records what its users do, so the organization holds personal information about employees and visitors. Under the Act respecting the protection of personal information in the private sector as amended by Law 25, supervised by the Commission d'accès à l'information du Québec, it must inform the people concerned, limit the collection to what is necessary for security, protect the data it collects (restricted access, for Val-des-Pins only the owner and the provider's technician, stored on NAS-01), and keep it no longer than needed (90 days at most in the register). The Civil Code of Québec (articles 35 to 41) protects private life, and capturing other people's communications without consent may be interception under section 184 of the Criminal Code; installing software on a device without express consent may violate section 8 of CASL (Canada's Anti-Spam Legislation). In the exposure register, facts about people (a phishing message opened in June) stay factual, minimal and about the asset; the person is never named, and the register is never used to observe or profile an individual. For this course the rule is simpler and stricter: you monitor systems and events, never people, only inside your own Authorized Lab Environment, with fictional data; you treat every capture, log, baseline and alert record as personal information — collect the minimum, keep it in the lab, delete it when the exercise is marked; you never enable promiscuous or monitor mode on a shared network; monitoring a partner, relative, roommate, classmate or colleague is never a course activity and may be a criminal offence (sections 6.3, 6.7 and 7.2).

              Why this is the expected answer. "respect for the confidentiality of the monitoring data collected" is a performance criterion of the whole competency, and every lab requires the section 9 legal and privacy statement.

              Essay 18 to 20

              Class 7 — Prioritizing monitoring activities

              0 / 3
              Essay 18Covers: Class 7 · Lesson 2.5.2 (Criticality) and 2.5.3 (Exposure)

              Explain the difference between criticality and exposure, how each is rated in this course, and why both are needed, using NAS-01 and PC-SHOP-01.

              Hint: consequences versus likelihood; FIPS 199 impacts 1–3 and the high-water mark; five factors E1–E5 and the 0–5 score; independence; review date.

              Model answer. Criticality measures how much the organization would suffer if the asset stopped doing its job or its data were disclosed or corrupted — a statement about consequences, not attackers. It is rated with the method of FIPS (Federal Information Processing Standards) 199: three impact questions (confidentiality, integrity, availability), each answered 1 limited, 2 serious, 3 severe; the criticality is the highest of the three (high-water mark); helpers are the RTO (Recovery Time Objective), the single point of failure and data classification (personal information gives a confidentiality impact of 3 without debate); the impact on the organization is rated, never the price, assets with the same data and role are rated as a group, and one sentence of justification is written per asset. Exposure measures how likely trouble is — the likelihood side of the risk equation (NIST SP 800-30): five observable facts scored 0 or 1 — E1 Internet contact, E2 known weakness (unsupported system, missing updates, default or shared password; the CVE (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures) list and the NVD (National Vulnerability Database) with its CVSS (Common Vulnerability Scoring System) score help), E3 people and media, E4 privilege (blast radius), E5 history in the last 12 months — summed to 0–5 and converted to the same 1–3 scale (0–1 Low, 2–3 Moderate, 4–5 High). NAS-01 is critical (3: a corrupted backup is discovered only on the day it is needed) but reached only by the nightly backup job, with one administrator account, current firmware and no incident — exposure score 1, Low. PC-SHOP-01 holds nothing of value (criticality 1) but allows browsing, runs an unsupported system, uses a shared account and had adware last year — score 4, High. Neither number alone places the two correctly, which is why exposure is independent of criticality and both are needed; exposure also changes (an update removes E2, E5 ages out, a remote-access rule adds E1), so every rating carries a review date.

              Why this is the expected answer. Criterion 2.3 requires prioritization "in accordance with network resources and security requirements"; the two ratings are how security requirements become a defensible order.

              Essay 19Covers: Class 7 · Lesson 2.5.4 (From two ratings to an order) · "priority score", "tiers", "fit", "reduced and deferred activities", "override"

              Describe how the ordered list of activities is produced and fitted into the resource envelope, and what happens to activities that do not fit.

              Hint: multiply; matrix; tiers; three tie-breakers; walk the sorted list; reduced activity before deferral; review date; override reasons.

              Model answer. The priority score of each asset is its criticality multiplied by its exposure (1 to 9); multiplication rather than addition, because an asset must be both critical and exposed to deserve continuous attention. The priority matrix (3 × 3 grid, a heat map) shows them all: 6–9 High, 3–4 Moderate, 1–2 Low. The score gives the tier — Tier 1 (6–9): continuous collection, immediate alerts, daily review, 90 days of retention; Tier 2 (3–4): continuous or periodic export, few alerts, weekly review, 30 days; Tier 3 (1–2): no dedicated collection, baseline check only. The order of work sorts by score, highest first, with three tie-breakers applied in sequence: higher criticality, then higher exposure, then the lower daily cost of the activity. The list is then fitted into the resource envelope (for Val-des-Pins 2,275 MB and 60 minutes per day): walk down the sorted list and add each activity while both running totals stay inside. When a Tier 1 activity does not fit, it is not dropped: a reduced activity is tried first — filtered logs instead of all logs, connection records instead of full packet capture (CNC-PC-01's capture went from 900 to 90 MB), sampling; what still does not fit becomes a deferred activity, an accepted gap written in the plan with its reason and a review date (October 16 in the example). The computed order is a proposal; the technician may override it with a documented reason — a dependency (NAS-01 is the recovery path of every Tier 1 asset) or a legal obligation (an asset holding personal information cannot be deferred without the owner's written decision) are accepted without argument; any other override is explained in the plan and signed by the owner. In the example the envelope ended at 1,875 MB (82 %) and 60 minutes (100 %), four activities deferred, one reduced, one override.

              Why this is the expected answer. This is criterion 2.3 executed end to end; section 6 of the Lab 1 plan is graded on exactly these mechanics.

              Essay 20Covers: Class 7 · Lesson 2.5.1 and 2.5.4 · "resource envelope", "Common beginner error", "Table 5 — the monitoring plan", "review cycle"

              Explain why "we will collect everything now and sort it out later" is wrong, define the resource envelope, and list the nine sections of the monitoring plan with the three events that trigger its review.

              Hint: storage, legal duty, quality of results; agreed with the owner, measurable units; sections 1 to 9; network change, incident, schedule.

              Model answer. Collected data that nobody reviews is worse than useless: it costs storage; it creates a legal duty, because logs and captures contain personal information that must be protected and deleted (sections 6.7 and 7.2); and it hides the few important events among millions of unimportant ones — the "quality of results" problem of Topic 6. An alert that nobody reviews protects nothing. The resource envelope is the total amount of each resource the organization has decided to dedicate to monitoring, expressed in measurable units — MB per day of storage with the retention period, minutes per day of analyst time, number of licences — agreed with the owner and written and dated in the plan; it is not the technician's private estimate (Val-des-Pins: 200 GB × 1024 ÷ 90 days ≈ 2,275 MB per day; 5 hours ÷ 5 days = 60 minutes per day). The plan's nine sections: 1 scope and network map; 2 constraints; 3 monitoring needs; 4 asset register (C, I, A, criticality, E1–E5, exposure, score, tier, justification, review date); 5 resource envelope; 6 ordered activities (rank, asset, activity, source, tool, MB/day, min/day, review frequency, owner, tier, status included / reduced / deferred); 7 exclusions and deferred activities (reason, decided by, date, review date); 8 review cycle; 9 legal and privacy statement (all data fictional; how captures and logs are stored, minimized and deleted). The plan is never finished: a change in the network (new asset, new Internet-facing service, new remote-access rule), an incident involving any asset (E5 becomes 1 and often reveals a wrong rating), and the fixed schedule (quarterly for a small business) trigger a review, at which the reference database is updated (Lesson 6.1) and deferred activities are reconsidered (Lesson 6.3).

              Why this is the expected answer. The monitoring plan is Deliverable 2 of Lab 1 and the document the whole of Topic 2 exists to produce.

              PART F

              Exam rules, expectations and closing checklist

              Part F

              Exam rules, expectations and closing checklist

              The mid-term (Class 10, Thursday, October 1, 2026) is written in class, on campus — one of only two on-campus meetings of the course. It counts for 25 % and, per the course outline, covers Topics 1 to 3 up to the selection of tools. Expect the same three families of questions as this review: multiple-choice, multiple-select with the number of answers stated, and short written answers, plus at least one case with a log extract or a small inventory to reason about.

              • Bring photo identification and a pen. Electronic dictionaries and cell phones are prohibited during tests (course outline). Nothing in the exam requires a computer.
              • Read the "(N correct answers expected)" of every multiple-select question and select exactly that number.
              • Write definitions with the course's words: preventative monitoring, event / alert / incident, baseline, false positive / false negative, constraint versus requirement, need versus alert versus tool, criticality versus exposure.
              • Show the arithmetic when a score is asked (impact × exposure; μ + 3σ; storage formula; envelope), and name the scale you are using — the four scoring methods of section A8.2 use different scales.
              • When a question gives evidence, answer from the evidence and name the question of the triage you are answering; never from the severity of the symptom.
              • Every legal statement in this course is general information, not legal advice (Legal Notice section 16); quote the section or the statute the lecture quoted, and no more.
              • A missed test with a valid reason permits a make-up; an absence of more than five days requires a medical certificate. Cheating and plagiarism result in failure of the assessment or the course and are reported in writing to the Dean (ISEP). The exam paper is confidential under section 17.2 of the Legal Notice: it is not shared, photographed or posted.

              Closing checklist — can you, from memory: state the definition of preventative monitoring and the seven pipeline stages; give the five elements of EZ01 and its achievement context; explain the two pass rules; classify a control as preventive, detective or corrective; name the three properties with one failure and one evidence each; explain what a hash proves; list the eight attack types with one trace each; give the five response steps; write the four triage questions and the four verdicts; classify a device into its family; read a /24 subnet; distinguish organizational from operational constraints and hard from soft; write a need in one sentence; compute criticality (high-water mark), exposure (E1–E5) and the priority score; name the three tie-breakers and the two override reasons; list the nine sections of the monitoring plan?
